speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a request to the Secretary of State for External affairs (Mr. Pearson), of which I gave him notice.
Would the minister care to comment on the important statement made by President Eisenhower yesterday on the subject of world peace?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN PRISONERS OF WAR
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MINISTERIAL COMMENT ON STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT EISENHOWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the president's statement to which the hon. member has referred is, I think, an inspiring and heartening declaration of the specific purposes and policies of the United States and as such it is of very great importance indeed. With the consent of the house it might be useful if I did put on the record one or two sentences from that statement because I think they embody principles to which we would be glad to subscribe in this house and in this country.
The president emphasized in his statement the "readiness of the free nations to welcome sincerely any genuine evidence of peaceful purpose enabling all peoples again to resume their common quest of just peace." Then he went on to state in this connection that a new leadership has assumed power in the Soviet union. "This new leadership," he said, "confronts a free world aroused, as rarely in its history, by the will to stay free," and "this free world knows-out of the bitter wisdom of experience-that vigilance and sacrifice are the price of liberty." Mr. Eisenhower then added:
This is the kind of free world which the new Soviet leadership confronts. It is a world that demands and expects the fullest respect of its rights and interests. It is a world that will always accord the same respect to all others.
The president stated that "the first great step along this way must be the conclusion of an honourable armistice in Korea," and that "this means the immediate cessation of
4006

Inquiries of the Ministry hostilities and the prompt initiation of political discussions leading to the holding of free elections in a united Korea." In that connection, Mr. Speaker, some additional hope has been given to the possibility.,, at least, of an armistice taking place by a unanimous decision of the United Nations political committee yesterday on a resolution on this subject.
The president went on to indicate in eloquent words that "the peace we seek, founded upon decent trust and co-operative effort among nations, can be fortified not by weapons of war but by wheat and by cotton; by milk and by wool; by meat and by timber and by rice. These are words that translate into every language on earth. These are needs that challenge this world in arms. This idea of a just and peaceful world is not new or strange to us." Then Mr. Eisenhower made a proposal which must, I am sure, arouse the interest of all peoples, to the effect that the United States government "is ready to ask its people to join with all nations in devoting a substantial percentage of the savings achieved by disarmament to a fund for world aid and reconstruction. The purposes of this great work," he added, "would be to help other peoples to develop the undeveloped areas of the world, to stimulate profitable and fair world trade, to assist all peoples to know the blessings of productive freedom." He said:
I know of nothing I can add to make plainer the sincere purpose of the United States.
This statement of purpose which I have just mentioned is one to which I am sure, Mr. Speaker, this house and the people of Canada would be glad indeed to subscribe.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 338, respecting co-operative credit associations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this act provides for the establishment of co-operative credit associations operating in more than one province under the supervision of the superintendent of insurance. Before any such national association may operate it will have to come to parliament for incorporation by a special act.
This legislation is introduced at this time because a group of provincial central cooperative societies has announced its intention to apply to parliament to be incorporated as a national co-operative association. It is the government's view that if parliament is to approve such legislation it is desirable that there be available suitable safeguards.
The main object of a national association will be the receiving of deposits from its members and the loaning of money to its members and making other approved investments. This is the fundamental function of provincial co-operative credit associations. Hon. members will realize that at certain times there will be surplus cash on deposit with a member operating in one part of the

Co-operative Credit Associations country while there may be a demand for loans in another part of the country. However, with the establishment of a co-operative credit association, it will be possible to loan surplus funds to members requiring cash for loans on a national basis thereby overcoming the present provincial limitation.
The members of an association will be cooperative credit societies incorporated by special act or declared by parliament to be eligible to become members of an association, not more than ten co-operative corporations (not being co-operative credit societies) and not more than fifteen natural persons.
It is provided that before an assocation commences accepting deposits and making loans it must obtain a certificate from the treasury board. This certificate will be granted only after the association has satisfied the board that it has complied with the provisions of the act.
The lending and investment powers of an association are subject to adequate safeguards in order to prevent its assets from being too heavily concentrated in one particular form and to preserve liquidity. For example, an association may not make any loan or investment if its cash on hand and on deposit with the chartered banks is less than five per cent of its own deposit liabilities.
There is provision for the appointment of auditors in a manner similar to that in the Bank Act. In addition there is a requirement for submitting annual reports to the government. The superintendent of insurance, who now has supervision over certain insurance, trust and loan companies, will have supervision over an association, and penalties are provided for violations of the provisions of this act.
I believe that hon. members are fully aware of the necessity of this legislation. The growth of co-operative credit societies in Canada in recent years has been widespread. As the operations of these organizations will undoubtedly include operations which are clearly of a banking nature, it is desirable that if these associations are going to operate on a national basis they should be under federal legislation as are the chartered banks.
I propose that when this bill receives second reading it be referred to the banking and commerce committee. At that time the superintendent of insurance and the officers of my department will be available to explain its provisions and discuss them with members of the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the principle of this bill. I believe the principle is simple, namely that of establishing, by law, provision for central credit societies. While I have not had the opportunity to look at the bill carefully, clause by clause, I feel that the principle is a good one. I for one can support second reading of the bill at this time. I believe that our credit unions have provided excellent credit facilities and a real service to the membership in the various credit unions in the different provinces in Canada.
Credit unions are in the intermediate and short-term credit field. They are prepared to lend money to their members, many of whom could not obtain loans through the regular lending facilities of the chartered banks. I feel that they have provided a very beneficial service, a service that is not provided and will not be provided to the same extent by the chartered banks.
Another thing, the membership of credit unions support the co-operative philosophy. They believe that by banding themselves together and forming a co-operative for the purpose of pooling their available cash so that it may be lent to their members upon application they are taking profits out of this particular business, namely, the lending of money. They feel that the philosophy of credit unions, the philosophy of co-operatives, is good and sound philosophy, and so they support credit unions not only because of the facilities they provide but because they believe in the principles behind co-operatives and credit unions.
I have had some experience in my own province with the workings of credit unions, and I know countless people who have been able to obtain money from credit unions without security, who would not have had any opportunity to obtain that money through chartered banks, and who, if they obtained the money from small loan companies, would have had to pay an excessive rate of interest. There are many farmer members of credit unions who have been able to borrow money to pay off their obligations when they had an opportunity to pay them at a considerably reduced amount because of a cash discount that was provided.

Co-operative Credit Associations These credit unions are making loans to their members tor the purchase of home furnishings, automobiles, farm machinery, and, as I said, have lent money for the purpose of paying off indebtedness on their property.
It is difficult for a single credit union to have the necessary reserves each and every year and each and every month of the year. So within the provinces, or within certain provinces, central credit societies have been established. In that central credit society the membership is composed of credit union associations. By a hundred or two hundred individual credit unions becoming members of the central society they can pool their funds; they can provide for credit unions that need a large amount of money for the purpose of loans, moneys in addition to that available in the local credit union.
This bill is merely extending the principle that now prevails in the central credit societies within the province. When this bill is finally passed, as I am sure it will be, and becomes the law of the country, and after credit unions have made available to them the provisions of the act by forming cooperative credit associations, I believe they will provide greater stability and greater security for the functioning of the various individual credit unions.
I have before me a publication of the Department of Agriculture for 1951 called "Credit Unions in Canada". It shows the very large number of Canadians who are now members of various credit unions in Canada. For example, in 1945, 590,000 Canadians were members of credit unions. By 1951, six years later, that number had almost doubled to
1,137,000	members. Credit union history is short in Canada; it extends back only 50 years, but progress has been rapid. In 1920, for example, there were only some 30,000 members in all the credit unions in Canada. That shows the phenomenal growth of credit unions and the fact that they are playing an increasingly important role in Canada.
I believe that credit unions are very desirable and that this bill will assist in the functioning of the credit unions in the various provinces. I know that the bill will be referred to the banking and commerce committee, where we shall have an opportunity to go over it clause by clause. If there are any questions on any specific items that we wish to raise I know that we shall have an opportunity to do so and shall receive a full explanation.
I am prepared to support the second reading of this bill today; but if it should be the desire of the house to postpone discussion to another day I would have no objection to that being done. My main interest is to

welcome the bill and to see that a bill of this kind becomes law in Canada, because I feel it will serve a very useful and important purpose.

I listened to what the minister said in his short statement. With his exposition of the principle of the bill I found myself in complete agreement. On behalf of my group I should like however to reserve the right to enter into a somewhat longer discussion of the bill at another time, if that can be arranged; when clause 1 is called in committee I presume that will be possible. We shall have an opportunity of studying the bill in the banking and commerce committee and of hearing any evidence that anyone wishes to give in that committee.
I support the principle of the bill; I think it is excellent. Anything that will strengthen and stabilize the individual credit unions throughout this country is good; it will help them to extend the services which they have been giving to the people of the country.
The credit unions, many of which are being organized every year throughout all of Canada, are organizations for the extension of short-term loans mainly to those who may require accommodation but who may not be considered to have enough of the kind of security that is asked for by the chartered banks. No source of small loans has as yet been provided for this type of borrower except by the small loan companies in Canada, and everybody knows that most of these small loan companies are nothing but loan sharks. They do prey upon the unfortunate who seem to have no other source of short-term financial assistance.
I want to say that anything we can do to extend and encourage the principle of cooperative self-help upon which credit unions are based is providing assistance to those people who now have to go to the loan sharks. Under the law of Canada these small loan companies are able to charge 24

per cent-they call it 2 per cent per month. But I want the house to know my investigation shows me that by compounding on their monthly balances they raise that interest to a rate of more than 30 per cent simple interest per year.

Mr. Speaker, co-operative credit unions hold a high position, and the government obviously is supporting that position by the introduction of this bill. I do not feel the bill will interfere particularly with the operation of commercial banks or with banking business generally because, as has been said before, these co-operative credit unions are not normally operating in the fields in which banks would be interested. The financing of the purchases of heavy machinery for individual farmers and for others is covered by farm improvement loans which have been instituted by the government.
It has been stated before that these unions cover a field which normally is not covered in any other way. My reason for believing that there is a certain amount of urgency in connection with the immediate passage of the bill, and the setting up of the legislation, is that these co-operative credit unions have a large amount of money on deposit, and they are and for some time have been making loans. They do not appear to fall into any classification under which they would be brought into line with normal banking procedure and banking regulations.
As I understand the principle of this bill, the intention is to do that. The bill gives protection to depositors who put money into these credit unions, and sets Up some sort of regulation as to what percentage can be lent to private individuals, without security, and what percentage must be held on deposit for reserve. This is timely legislation. I think it should be hurried through as quickly as possible, because even the co-operative

This is a wonderful movement, and I regret time does not permit our giving more careful consideration to a measure of this kind which has historic significance. However, since the minister appears to be adamant, and we have no recourse except to accept his dictatorial decision that we go ahead this morning, even though the heavens fall, I should like to say a few words about this great movement.
The debate on this measure affords an opportunity to pay a tribute to the marvellous work accomplished by St. Francis Xavier university in Nova Scotia in creating what has been known throughout the world as the Antigonish movement, in which the chief workers have been the Rev. Dr. Coady and Father Tompkins, or Dr. Jimmy Tompkins as he was popularly known throughout the maritimes, as well as in Newfoundland.
These men between them acquired a great knowledge of the business of, and an insight into the needs of the workers, the farmers and the fishermen, in their respective environments. They had the ability to inspire those people to assist themselves. I do not know how far hon. members are familiar with the humble beginnings this movement had in Nova Scotia. In the days of the depression following the first world war, when the fishermen did not know what to do to earn a dollar, Dr. Tompkins came to them with the idea that they might help themselves, and showed them that if they would pool their resources and ship their lobsters alive to the Boston market they would get a greater return. Soon they would be able to lift themselves out of the depression and poverty which had been their lot for generations.
One can imagine the enthusiasm with which they greeted the first cheque returning from the Boston market showing them that they had received many times more for their produce than they would have received had they carried on in the traditional way and sold to the merchants. This credit union movement, which deals with money, sprang from that humble beginning in the little village of Canso. The credit union movement has spread throughout the country as well as in the United States. In that country they have a national association with headquarters at Madison, Wisconsin. Their organization is known as CUNA, the Credit Unions National Association.
There is another feature about the movement that is of particular interest, in that there is complete harmony between the members of credit societies in this country and those in the United States. Not only is there harmony, but fraternity, co-operation, and an anxiety and willingness to help


one another. It is a marvellous movement and one which is not merely confined to dollars and cents. When you are dealing with a co-operative it is not like going to a banker who will look at you with a cold eye trying to appraise your resources. When you go to a co-operative credit union officer you go to a person who is a friend, and if he possibly can, he is going to find a way by which he can help you, not only in such cases as were mentioned by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) but also in the case of medical and hospital expenses, money for holidays and for the building of houses. Money has been furnished in all these instances by such credit societies.
The growth of the movement in Nova Scotia, particularly in the island of Cape Breton, has been miraculous. I have seen houses being built there co-operatively which were financed partly through co-operative credit societies or credit unions. People obtained loans from the credit union to buy the land and they all worked together to build their homes. These societies have financed the building of many homes in the island of Cape Breton and in other places where the movement exists.
The progress of the movement in the province of Quebec is not so well known to members who do not come from that province. They may not be so familiar with what has happened there. The growth of the credit union movement or caisse populaire in the province of Quebec has been astonishing. It exists all throughout the province and is just as much a part of the business life of the communities as the banks themselves. While I recognize the desirability of having legislation to provide for the proper inspection and supervision of' a national movement of this kind, yet I feel, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, that it is a pity that we have not had more time to go into the matter. I am only speaking now extemporaneously and without giving any lengthy consideration to the matter, but I want to repeat that it is a marvellous movement and anybody who has been connected with it knows that. The spirit that can be and has been developed amongst members of co-operative societies wherever they have been established and the benefits that have been brought to the members are really astonishing.
I think of a case now of a man who came to me last summer and asked me for a loan. I said, "Do you not belong to the civil service co-operative credit society?" As I happened to be one of the prime movers in establishing it, I knew all about it. He said, "No." I said, "All you have got to do is to

go to the treasurer and ask for a loan and you will get it in a very short time without any trouble at all. I will tell you what I will do. I will send you to the treasurer and you go there, join the credit society, ask for a loan, and see what happens." He went to the treasurer and got his loan. I have seen that happen many times.
It is a marvellous thing for people with large families who get into financial difficulties and are not able to go to the bankers. They cannot go to the bankers but they go to their friends in the credit society. It is a pity that this movement is not better known, and I am astonished that it is not when one realizes how important it is.
I am sure that careful consideration will be given to the clauses of the bill in the banking and commerce committee, and I only regret that time does not permit us to give greater attention to it at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words regarding this bill, which we have not had time to study. Following the comments I have heard, may I say that in my opinion, this bill will render new services and facilitate the development of co-operative credit associations, that is our "caisses populaires" as we call them in Quebec, our credit unions.
Mr. Chairman, I have taken an active interest in the credit union movement for the past fifteen years or so. I myself founded a credit union of which I was manager for seven years. As you are no doubt aware, credit unions were started in the province of Quebec over forty years ago by Commander Alphonse Desjardins, and they have been greatly beneficial to the rural and working people.
The credit union movement in the province of Quebec stems almost entirely from good citizenship and the practice of the virtue of charity. That is why in the last fifteen years or so, the number of credit unions has increased threefold and their capital has expanded from thirty or forty million to the present total of approximately $300 million, if I remember well.
I hope that the bill now before the house will not interfere with the development of the "caisses populaires" in the province of


Quebec nor dampen the spirit of collaboration that must exist between those and the credit unions in other provinces. I like to think that the government, before introducing this new bill, was wise enough to consult experienced people who were anxious to safeguard, so to speak, the autonomous character of the "caisse populaire" of the province of Quebec.
The services rendered by credit unions, as I said a moment ago, have been extremely valuable to the people. I would like to point out to the members of this house, for their guidance, that the first loan granted by the "caisse populaire" at Dolbeau was a $10 loan. It enabled a poor workingman, who was then earning only $15 a week, to pay the hospital a $25 bill. When he handed in the $10 which had been lent him by the "caisse populaire", he managed to settle this $25 account, thus saving $15, plus charges. Later on he paid back the credit union through bi-monthly one dollar payments, with almost no interest charges whatever. He therefore managed to get rid of this debt at no hardship to his own family. On another occasion, thanks to the Dolbeau credit union, about twenty citizens of that community were enabled to build houses, through loans of approximately $300. Of course this was some years ago when construction costs were lower than they are these days. The credit union made loans of $300, the borrower buying materials for that sum until there was no money left. Then he came back for another $300 loan. In this way the credit unions caused a large number of houses to be built.
They are still rendering extremely useful services in a field where banking institutions are unable to act. In the case of larger loans, the banks must require repayment within 12 months, while co-operative credit unions grant their borrowers the privilege of repaying these sums according to their means. In other words they may repay a $2,000 loan through monthly payments of $25.
It is with pleasure that I have taken this opportunity to say a word about our "caisses populaires"-co-operative credit unions-in Quebec, for they perform very laudable work and have rendered great services. Therefore, I hope that under this bill our credit unions may be able to increase the services they have already rendered in Quebec since their inception.

The credit union is just another manifestation of the co-operative idea. It is the manifestation of that idea applied to the lending of money. As an active teacher a number of years ago I was one of the first members and, if I remember rightly, I was the president of the first teachers' credit union in my own city of Saskatoon. Many other groups of employees, for instance the employees on our newspaper there, have credit unions of their own. The credit union is only an instance of people helping each other and by so doing directly helping themselves.
Another thing which has perhaps been mentioned here already is that these unions tend to keep the small borrower out of the hands of the small lending companies whose reputation as far as I can see-although I have had no direct connection with them nor direct experience with them-is not always so savoury. Small people are fortunate in not having to rely on such institutions when they can lend each other money as the occasion requires and then receive it back. If there is any profit in the matter may I say that it is not profit in the ordinary sense of the word but rather a saving to them through their work.
For these reasons I have great pleasure in supporting this bill and I shall look forward with some interest to studying the details.

This bill today is the means, on a national scale, of tying up all these community and provincial organizations which, in my opinion, will be a challenge to the regular banking system of this country in the days to come. It at least has driven them into the small loans field. All these new chains, like the Household Finance and many others which exist today, are attempts to duplicate or offset the credit union movement.
When the industrial development bank was proposed in this house, I said that it was a waste of time to establish another branch of the chartered banks which would merely underwrite doubtful investments in the aftermath of the war. I have one answer I should give the hon, member for Greenwood in reply to his question yesterday about major construction projects. I mentioned in my speech that we had 1,048 major construction contracts. By this we mean contracts involving more than $10,000. They vary from several million down to $10,000. We have information available for each of the three services, navy, army and air force, detailing each major construction contract showing the items comprising the contract with the expenditure incurred as known at the end of the year. That is the end of the calendar year, December 31, 1952. A great part of this information has already been put before the defence expenditure committee, and if anything further is desired it can be dealt with there in detail.
A breakdown of construction contracts which might be useful here is that showing those supervised by Defence Construction Limited or other agencies which constitute the major construction contracts. We have no major construction contracts that are let by the Department of National Defence itself. They are handled for us by Defence Construction Limited or by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The only contracts that we supervise are those for renovation, repair, alteration and the like, and most of these are under $10,000. The number and value of major construction contracts since April 1, 1950, are: major contracts supervised by other agencies, 968; under construction during 1952-53, 749. Major contracts supervised by the Department of National Defence, total 1,100; under construction 1952-53, 299. The totals are 2,068, or under construction in 1952-53, 1,048, the figure I gave at the outset.
In addition there are contracts for married quarters which are constructed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is responsible for design, layout of the contract, inspection and supervision.
The question of standard buildings was raised, and it was suggested that in view of the fact that we use to a great extent standard building designs that have been worked out, we shall not require the service of consultants. This unfortunately is not so. The standard buildings have to be modified to suit the site condition. This involves the design of foundation in each case. There also has to be supervision by engineers and architects during the course of construction
Supply-National Defence for which they receive the fees that are set by the architectural association and which are current in civilian practice. I might point out that in major construction in apartment housing, it is estimated that rather more than 50 per cent of the cost today goes for what is called engineering, a much bigger proportion than in building up to recent times. Therefore, in almost every case it is necessary to have an engineer. The normal design fee in commercial and industrial practice for individual buildings is 3 to 4 per cent of the cost.
Owing to the use of standard buildings as high a percentage as this is not usually paid for design in the case of buildings for the Department of National Defence. For example, in the case of 460 standard buildings constructed by the R.C.A.F. from standard designs the consultant fee paid represented approximately 1 [DOT] 5 per cent of the cost, or much less than half of the cost usually paid by civilian purchasers on individual contracts. Already the total number of buildings constructed or being constructed to designs which are standard is 754. One design has been used 45 times, and 27 designs have been used 10 or more times each, so that this practice of having standard designs, which we started as far back as 1948, has paid off very substantially from the point of view of saving money and also of speed in getting on with the job.
I should add in answer to the question about the commissioning of ships, it is hoped that eight new minesweepers will be commissioned in 1953-54.

I should like to inquire first about the educational standards required in the army, and the way in which they have been changed. Some time ago I placed a question on the order paper, to which I received an answer on February 5. In that question I asked the following:
1.	What are the educational standards at present required for enlistment in the (a) navy; (b) army; (c) air force?
2.	On what date were these educational requirements put into effect?
The answer I received dealing with the standards required by the army was as follows:
The suitability of applicants for enrolment in the Canadian army is tested by aptitude and intelligence tests.
In other words there are no educational requirements at all. As a matter of fact I understand that a certain number of men who were unable to read or write were taken into the army. On the other hand the educational requirements of the navy stipulate the completion of elementary schooling. The
Supply-National Defence same applies to the air force, except for aircrew, where junior matriculation is required.
Why were the educational requirements for the army abolished on November 13, 1951? How can men who cannot read or write, and who are taken into the army, be usefully employed; because, in the light of the technical development that has taken place in that branch of the service, it would seem to me that educational requirements equal to those of the navy or the air force are necessary in the army for practically all jobs, particularly those jobs in any of the technical corps.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I have never heard of there being in the Canadian army any soldier who could not read or write. If the hon. member has knowledge of that, it is news to me. Such a case has never been brought to my attention. I have never heard such a suggestion before, and I would doubt it very much.
I would agree with him that it is quite inconceivable that useful work could be found for anyone in any of the three services who could not read and write. The educational standards are precisely the same as those for the soldiers in the second world war, namely the aptitude test and the M-test, and the same score is now required as was required at that time.
It is difficult to relate a common educational standard to school grades. It is even difficult to talk in terms of grades because there are ten provinces in Canada and the grades, as we find, do not correspond. Generally speaking, however, a man who passes the aptitude test and gets the required score is likely to have at least sixth grade and probably more likely seventh. In the navy and air force the educational requirements are just about the same. They both use a combination of grade measurements and aptitude tests.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if it is not a fact that up to the 13th of November, 1951, there was an educational requirement of elementary schooling, in the army as well as in the other two services, which has now been abolished. He has not explained really why there should be this difference between the services.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: At the time of Korea, in June, 1950, we had raised the standards to a very high level because we were getting more men than were needed to provide for the planned build-up of the three services, and intake was controlled by raising the standards. However, in the case of the 25th and 27th brigades we applied the wartime standard and that has been applied since.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I want to get at this point. Is this one of the cases in which the standardization as between the three forces, which was

Supply

National Defence put into effect some years ago, has now been departed from?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: No; it was never achieved. The three services each had their own methods of selection, There is a committee which has worked on common standards but the navy and air force prefer to keep their own separate systems because of different requirements, including a higher proportion of other ranks in the navy and air force able to take technical training, and I mean technical in the precise sense, to train as artificers, mechanics and electricians. In view of the fact that these standards were well worked out and well known in the three services, I did not feel anything was to be gained by making them uniform- In fact we would have lost rather than gained by it.

speechtext: In a dispatch by Bill Boss a few days ago I noticed that the great majority of the people in the brigade had educational attainments of less than grade 8, and that a considerable amount of work was being done, or proposed to be done, to provide education for these people in the army. Can the minister tell us what progress has been made? According to the article, the majority of afternoons are spent in educational activities and so forth. Has the minister any definite figures as .to how m.uch the educational standards of the men of that brigade have been^raised? I think it is, an excellent thing- to be doing.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I made a statement on this matter the; other night in [DOT] answer to the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: So that there will be no repetition, perhaps I might interject, that what I want more particularly is the number of people taking educational work and what progress has been made.	*	.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I would have tp get the precise information from abroad. We have arrangements made under which education is carried on by. correspondence courses in the same way. as during the second world war when the .system was organized by the Canadian Legiop,. which, had. an excellent committee on the subject under the chairmanship of Colonel Wilfrid Bovey, who is well known to a number of hon. members. We have carried that on since with the co-operation of the Canadian Legion and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
My recollection is that at the present time there are about 1,500 courses being taken. In the case of the 27th brigade, it would probably be a fair estimate that the other ranks are all about grade 8. If you consider the matter, that is a very good grade indeed for peacetime forces and for people engaged in corresponding work in civilian life. The men there are encouraged to take voluntary work and we


are instituting a system whereby compulsory education is given to other ranks to bring them up to grade 8 as a minimum. That is just being instituted now. The facts I gave are to be found at page 3924 of Hansard for April 15. There are 5,360 serving personnel taking D.V.A. courses in the army alone.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: It seems to be almost one o'clock, and I want to discuss with the minister the question of housing at Wainwright camp. J wonder if we might call it one o'clock.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot be here at 2.30. I would be glad to answer the hon. member because I have been at Wainwright camp.	...

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
For quite a few months the
question of housing in the town of Wainwright has been under discussion and has been causing quite a little dissatisfaction. Because of the building up of the camp over past years there has been quite a heavy influx of civilian personnel with their families into the town of Wainwright. As a result thereof and because there is insufficient accommodation, it has made it particularly hard for some of the residents of Wainwright who do not have their own homes, and the necessary housing is not available. On the 12th of February I received a letter from the secretary. of; the Wainwright and . district chamber of commerce and agriculture, dealing with this matter. He reported that at a recent meeting they had representations from ' the Wainwright branch of the Amalgamated -Civil Servants of Canada with respect to the matter.	. -	*
The chamber pointed out to these representatives that the, only reason for the high rents and lack; of accommodation was that the camp was not a permanent one. I asked the minister about the matter, of permanency a couple of weeks ago and he told me it was permanent, in the same w,ay as Camp ipeta-wawa and pertain other camps are permanent. But apparently that has not fixed the trouble. Is any provision being made by the department to provide housing for married men on the permanent staff there and also for civilians working in the camp in a civilian capacity?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
As I said in answer to the hon. member the other day, Wainwright is a permanent camp, but we do not expect to have large units or numbers of soldiers there permanently. It is to be used for training units in field operations. These will be sent there, as has been done in the past two summers, for periods of one, two, three or four months. Generally speaking they wi)

be under active service conditions and will be engaging in field operations on a very large scale.
Therefore we do not plan to have a very large permanent staff in the camp the year round. In the winter the camp will be used for winter exercises as was done, for example, in preparation for exercise Sweetbriar when we had some 2,200 men there for ten days. But it will not be used in the same way as Petawawa or Camp Borden where troops are stationed permanently. Therefore it will not have a large permanent staff. The staff who will be living there throughout the winter will be the minimum necessary to keep the buildings and the camp going. So far we have 26 permanent married quarters for which contracts have been placed. If we see any need for building any more we will build them, but so far that need has not been seen. Generally speaking, it is not our practice to build married quarters for civilian employees. We think that it is difficult enough for us to be in the landlord business on the scale we are with regard to service personnel Without going into it for civilians as well. It is very unusual for us to have 'civilians in married quarters.	,
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The'committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at one o'clock I was endeavouring to seture from the Minister of National Defence some favourable consideration with regard to the housing situation for permanent officers and for those people who have moved into Wainwright in order to work at the camp. The information I received from the minister was not very satisfactory. He pointed out that the camp was mainly used for three or four months during the summer, and was occupied in the wintertime by a staff of caretakers, if one could use that term. He did not feel that the department wanted to provide homes for the people concerned with civilian work at the camp. The people of Wainwright are not satisfied with that explanation.
I pointed out to the minister that I received a letter from the Wainwright and district chamber of commerce and agriculture informing me of the delegation from the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, and that letter in part reads as follows:
The chamber could only inform the delegation that high rents were due to two things: first, to the inability of the town to provide rent accommodation for more than a small fraction of those who
Supply-National Defence desired it; and, second, the failure of the depart* ment of defence to make Wainwright a permanent military camp.
Much rental property, some of it of a very unsatisfactory nature, has been provided by the permanent residents at considerable cost. As long as the use of the camp as a permanent training grounds remains in doubt, the owners of this rental property will seek to recover their capital investment in as short a time as possible to avoid serious loss. It would seem, therefore, that it is the duty of the government of Canada to protect their employees against excessive rents by providing a proper amount of competitive housing in order to force rents down to a more reasonable figure. If the department of defence would provide living quarters for married personnel on the permanent staff of the camp, the same result would be achieved.
The letter goes on to say that the rents being charged are very high, and in some cases there, is a dearth of the most elemental conveniences, and then adds:
Therefore, the morale of those who live in town is generally low. It is particularly unfortunate that our men in uniform should feel Unfairly treated in their own country. The high ideal of the western allies in the "cold war" must lose some of its idealism in the eyes of those who, understandably, become disgruntled. '
After the delegation went back and discussed the matter again with their own organization, I received this resolution from the secretary of the Wainwright branch of the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, under the; heading "Housing-Wainwright, Alberta." It reads as follows:
Whereas, the present housing and rooming shortage in the town of Wainwright, Alberta has led to exorbitant rentals being charged for existing inferior accommodation; and
Whereas, the Wainwright chamber of commerce and agriculture maintain that this condition is due to two things; first, the inability of the towh to provide rental accommodation for moVe than a small fraction of those who desire it; and second, to the failure of the Department of National Defence to make Wainwright a permanent military camp; and
Whereas, it is generally agreed that the town of Wainwright cannot, under these temporary conditions, adequately take care of the influx of both arfny and government civilian personnel seeking accommodation; therefore
Be it resolved: That the government, oil behalf of the said army and government civilian personnel, investigate immediately the housing conditions in Wainwright and render all possible assistance in the promotion of a low rental housing scheme to alleviate present conditions.
I may say that condition has existed for many months, and the troubles are not yet cleared up. I was hoping that today I would get some encouragement from the minister with regard to this matter. In any event, his answer was not very satisfactory.
While I am dealing with this subject, perhaps I should deal also with the matter of education of the families of these men in the military camp as well as the families of those civilian workers who moved into Wainwright, seeking work at the camp itself.
4024	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence This movement has been the cause of a lack of accommodation in the schools which is costing the school board a great deal of extra expense. The board is now compelled to build more classrooms because of the presence of these people in the town who are not by any means permanent. As soon as the work at the camp is completed, then these people will move out again. I was wondering whether or not the government has considered giving any assistance in this connection. Perhaps the associate minister could give me some information on that, and then I may have one or two more questions to ask.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
As has already been
intimated to the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, the department seeks, so far as possible, to house its permanent service staffs at permanent camps, and those civilians who must necessarily remain at the camp practically all the time. Otherwise, the department tries to engage local civilians on the civilian side and most of these people look after their own housing needs. I might say that the situation at Wainwright is under consideration at the moment, and the particulars which the hon. member has mentioned will be considered and discussed with the housing authorities. Until now there have not been enough service children permanently located at Wainwright to justify considering school facilities, but I can assure the hon. member that both the problems which he has mentioned are being reviewed.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I thank the minister for that information. I hope that no time elapses in having both these matters investigated, because I do know from the letters I have received, and from a personal visit there not many months ago, that conditions are not satisfactory. The additional number of children present in the town as a result of workers moving in to take part in the building program at the camp has caused the members of the school board to make provision for additional classrooms. I believe those rooms are to be built just as soon as it is possible to do so. I think the department has some responsibility in that connection. If we should have peace in Korea-which is hoped for by many people, although not by some-then the camp may be closed or perhaps cut down materially. That would leave the ratepayers of the Wainwright school division putting up money that would not be necessary. I therefore hope that the department will see to it that an early investigation is made and that something definite is done to relieve those conditions which I have brought to the attention of the department.
There is another matter with respect to which I have had questions on the order


paper for some time, namely the supply of milk to the Wainwright camp. I have asked for the price being charged to the camp during 1950, 1951, 1952 and 1953 to date. I understand an exorbitant price is being charged there, and I wanted to have that understanding confirmed before saying anything further about it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I have not particulars of any contracts of that nature. I assume that tenders for milk supply would be called for and contracts let by the Department of Defence Production. The Department of National Defence would not necessarily have the details of any of those contracts. The question should be addressed to the Department of Defence Production.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I have placed those questions on the order paper. 1 realize that the departmental officials have been extremely busy providing information for the defence expenditure committee that is now sitting dealing with these matters, but I hope that information will be brought down soon because I want to say something about the matter before the session closes.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Last evening the minister promised me an answer to a question I asked. Possibly the associate minister could give it today. It is in connection with the amount paid for 14 minesweepers. I suggested to him that the cost of these was estimated as $950,000 each whereas the actual cost was $3 million each. The minister promised to look the matter up and let me know today. I have not received the answer.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: With reference to the hon. member's question, may I say that I understand the figure of approximately $900,000-

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: -was not really an estimate of the completed cost of a minesweeper. It was only a preliminary estimate of the first elements, which go to make up a minesweeper. The ancillary things which go to make up a minesweeper's equipment and armaments, etc., were not included. The figure was in other words the initial estimate of the partial cost of a minesweeper. I am told that the cost of a completed minesweeper of the type to which the hon. member referred is in the order of $3 million.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Is that not an extraordinarily large discrepancy? I refer to the difference between $950,000 and $3 million?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
What I endeavoured to tell the hon. gentleman was that the $950,000 figure was not really at any time a full estimate of a completed minesweeper. It was a

preliminary estimate made of the first elements of a minesweeper when the construction program was being set up. It was not the full estimate of the cost of a completed minesweeper at any time.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am not disputing what the minister says. But was it not announced, at the original time the announcement was made of this fact, that the cost would be $950,000?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Not to my knowledge. I have no recollection of any announcement to that effect.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: That is not an answer at all.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Greenwood asked for some further information from the minister during the morning session. He asked what were the number of construction projects involving a cost of a quarter of a million dollars or more. The figures which I have been given show that from April 1, 1950, to February 28, 1953, the number of such projects was as follows:	In
the navy 29, having a dollar value in the aggregate of $28,579,438; in the air force 319, having a dollar value of $364,035,050; and in the army 102, having a value in dollars of $88,042,107; or a total of 450 projects having an aggregate dollar value of $480,674,595.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope hon. members on the other side of the chamber will not think anything has gone wrong with me when I say that I am rising to extend a compliment to the Department of National Defence. It arises out of a matter which a number of hon. members have referred to during the course of this discussion with regard to the army estimates. I refer to the provision which is being made, or which some members feel should yet be made, with repect to the education of children of service people stationed permanently in various locations.
The compliment I wish to extend is in respect of the arrangement made between the Department of National Defence and the school board of the city of Winnipeg. As the associate minister knows, the department has stationed a large number of service personnel permanently at the Fort Osborne barracks. That fact created a tremendous problem for the school board of the city of Winnipeg. Perhaps I must qualify my compliment by saying that negotiations seemed to be unusually protracted and that the chairman and the members of the school board of Winnipeg thought at times that it was taking too long to complete the arrangement. However, when the arrangement was finally completed, it was highly satisfactory. It involved, in
Supply-National Defence the main, a considerable contribution of federal money to the school board of the city of Winnipeg in order to enable it to put up the necessary building and to provide the necessary equipment.
I may say further that the members of the school board of the city of Winnipeg are perfectly satisfied that there will be no interference with their handling of the affairs of this new school and that there is no interference with provincial jurisdiction over education involved in this financial assistance. In other words, I rise to offer this compliment and I express the hope that other members who are concerned with similar problems in their locality will take heart from the fact that in this case a satisfactory agreement was concluded. Of course, we have an extremely progressive group of people on the school board of the city of Winnipeg, and they pressed the matter until there was this satisfactory agreement. I want to say also- as I said the other day-that in a case like this we are glad to know that the government's reluctance to provide federal aid to education did not interfere with the need for dealing with this problem. We in the city of Winnipeg are pleased with the arrangement, and we hope that this principle of federal financial aid to education will be extended.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I wish to thank the hon. member for his kindly words.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to ask a few questions of the associate minister. They arise out of a return that was tabled yesterday concerning welfare services. I have a fairly comprehensive report on the present situation of welfare in the various services. Question No. 2 reads:
What staff at unit level is detailed exclusively to welfare service duty in (a) Korea; (b) Germany?
I find that the reply indicates that one officer and an assistant is delegated exclusively to welfare work. My specific question is this. Does that indicate that there is on foot a move to militarize welfare services? It seems to me that formerly there was no officer designated as such for welfare services. My question is, does it mean that welfare is going to become an integral part of the military organization?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
In response to the specific question, it is my information that in each battalion or equivalent unit-I know it was so when I was in Korea a year or more ago-there is an officer and an assistant who is delegated to carry out what might be included in the general term of welfare duties in that unit. I think that has been
4026	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the established practice and has been fairly generally used for quite some time.
The question of welfare, as the hon. member knows, is one that is under continual study, and up until the present time it has been felt, after much study and consideration, that to carry on these services within the service itself-the army in this case-is the most satisfactory way of handling the situation in the circumstances which obtain at the present time in our Canadian army.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: It does not necessarily mean that it is going to be a process of militarizing welfare. If voluntary services would appear to do a better job, they might be resorted to, if circumstances change?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I think it would be fair to say this. In the consideration of this problem there is no intention at all, as the hon. member puts it, to militarize welfare services. If we are convinced at any time that whatever arrangement is worked out by study and experimentation could be improved upon, we shall give consideration to that fact, but up to the present we have felt that the present method of handling that part of the interests of the troops is best.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to bring up the matter of desertions. I got a return on December 18 which showed that at that time a total of 2,005 persons were listed as deserters from the armed services. There is an article in the Calgary Herald of November 29 which bears that out. I will read part of it. It says that the armed services really make no efforts to apprehend deserters or to deal with them. This particular article deals with a soldier who came back from Korea. He was a deserter for some three or four months during that period. Whilst he was a deserter he drew $260 in gratuities which were paid over to him anyhow. He went across the border through our immigration people, and so forth, came back and eventually, after several months, gave himself up. After dealing with all these circumstances the article says:
During that time-
That is the time that this man was a deserter. I continue:
During that time my acquaintance was making fruitless attempts to persuade the army to collect its missing soldier, providing them with information Which would have made it quite simple for him to be picked Up. At no time did the army display the slightest interest in the matter, and one letter from, the adjutant-general's department in Ottawa makes the astounding statement that "the primary responsibility of an absentee of the Canadian army is for him to return to his unit or to the nearest
Canadian army establishment"	It is in the
absentee's interest to report as soon as possible and thus terminate his offence.	*	'


The comment on that is:
This is like saying that it is the duty of all offenders against the laws to surrender themselves to the police.
What steps are taken by military authorities, by the department, to apprehend deserters and to cut down on the number of deserters? The number of 2,005 is quite a large one; in fact it is approximately a little more than 2 per cent of the total number in the services, or it was at the time this article was published.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The question of deserters of course is a serious one in any service. I suppose it is reasonable to say that it is likely to be much more common in a cold war than in a hot war. The problem is with us, and I am informed that we do try to apprehend all deserters. But as to the degree of the effort that is put into the search, the number of people required in the provost corps to carry on such duties in addition to their regular duties is an important consideration. Generally speaking, we do apprehend as many as we can as quickly as we can. The figure of 2,005 quoted by the hon. member includes I am told a considerable number of deserters who have since been apprehended. Naturally I do not know the specific facts about the case to which the hon. member has just referred.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: On that point, the statement in this return put out by the department is that the deserters not subsequently apprehended or returned to duty were 2,005.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: As of that time, yes; but we still continue to apprehend them as fast as we can, and have obtained a good many of them since, I am told. I am also advised that in connection with the apprehension of deserters the provost corps work with local police in the cities and provinces and also with the R.C.M.P., and that they do continue at all times to search for the missing men.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: What does the minister say about this article I have just quoted, which states that the soldier's absence and his situation, where he was staying, were reported to the army and no action was taken.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Frankly I would not say anything until I looked at the case and the file.
I do not want to express an opinion on an excerpt from a newspaper article, but if the hon. member will give me particulars I will have the matter looked into. I would not care to comment further on the case until I know more about the actual facts.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I'have a question which has to do with this problem. A lot of the service personnel returning from Korea arid being

discharged from the 27th brigade are boys who went into the service with no previous employment. They are now coming out of the service and they are still unemployed. The government has set up a system whereby their unemployment insurance credits are paid for them while in the service, but when they register for employment or unemployment insurance, it is necessary that their record of credits come down from Ottawa to the unemployment insurance commission office. I have had cases myself that go back over the last year. In one case the boy had anywhere from two months to five months of his unemployment insurance commission credits returned to the local office. I have had considerable correspondence with the defence department, and I do not think the trouble is there because the mechanics that have to be gone through are that national defence reports the discharge. Then veterans affairs have something to do with it, but in the final analysis it must come through to the Department of Labour. I have seen boys who were married and unemployed who waited all that time to get those credits through. Is any progress being made in linking up the three departments necessary to get these credits through as quickly as possible?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Speaking on behalf of the unemployment insurance commission, this is the first time that such a complaint has come to my attention. For my part we will certainly look into it to see what can be done to prevent any delays of that kind occurring in the future.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I have written the minister's department, through the deputy minister, and apparently there is no co-ordination there. I do not know where the roadblock is, but it is somewhere between national defence and the Department of Labour.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I should be glad to look into it.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: To return to this matter of deserters, the total number listed as not having been apprehended at November 20, 1952, for the previous year was 2,005. Can the minister tell me how many of these have been subsequently apprehended, and what is the total number of people listed as deserters at the present time?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I will try to get that information later.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister some questions regarding two pieces of army property. The first of my questions is concerned with tbe armouries at 'Quebec dity. I noticed, according to an article in
Supply~i-National Defence the Ottawa Journal of February 11, that there had been three explosions in the armouries in that city. The implication in the report, as I understood it, was to the effect that while the authorities did not wish to express any official opinion at that time, they did use words which raised the question as to whether or not those explosions had been set, or whether they were accidental. I am particularly interested in knowing whether anything has been found out since that time which would establish whether they were deliberately set, and the damage done by the explosions.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am informed there were three separate fires which originated in the armoury to which the hon. member has referred. I think no great damage was done; but each of those fires is now being investigated. I have no report as to the causes of any of the three fires as yet.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Was I correct in understanding that the words used were to the effect that it was felt investigations might establish that they were set deliberately? If so, has anything further developed?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I think that was the view of a newspaper. We will have no definite views in the department until we receive a report.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
The impression left by the article was that it had been based on a statement by the authorities. Would the minister let the committee know, as soon as he can, what the exact situation is?
Then I have a further question concerning the ordnance depot at Plouffe park. It has come to my attention during this week that certain buildings there are being dismantled. They are not part of the main structure, although they are within the fence around the depot. These are buildings which, I understand, were erected at some considerable cost, and they are now in process of being dismantled. What is the reason for their dismantling, and what did it cost to erect them?
