maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I have two questions to ask the minister, the first of which has to do with benevolent funds. It has been my understanding that men who have served in Korea with the army do not have the same privileges in the matter of benevolent funds as are available to the men from the air force and the navy. On March 30 answers were tabled to the following question I had uSksdi
1.	Are veterans with Korean service eligible tor assistance from the navy, army and air force benevolent funds?
2.	Is there a difference in the treatment of such veterans depending on the branch of the service to which they belong?
3.	If so. for what reason is such distinction made?
The answers I received were as follows:
1. (a) Canadian naval service benevolent trust fund: Yes.
So it appears that the Korean veterans of the navy have the widest possible privileges. The answers continue:
(b) Army benevolent fund: No.
The army benevolent fund was established by act of parliament to administer funds remaining from canteen operations during the second world war. It provides assistance for veterans who served in the Canadian army during the period September, 1939 to September, 1946. To be eligible for benefits, a Korean veteran must also have served during the above period.
Then, the answer in respect of the air force was that their veterans were eligible. From these answers it would seem clear that a difference is made, and that the young lads who served in the army in Korea cannot get any help from the army benevolent fund.
During the discussion of the estimates on April 15 the Minister of National Defence made a brief statement on the point, which is reported at page 3928 as follows:
I should add, however, that it has been decided to institute a Canadian army welfare fund similar to the benevolent funds for the air force and navy for the purpose of extending benefits to serving personnel. That has been set up and a statement to that effect will go out tonight.
Will the associate minister tell us exactly what provision has been made, and the method in which these funds are to be made available to the Korean army veterans?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
The statement by the hon. member is essentially correct. The difference in utility of the benevolent funds depends upon the terms of charters under which they were organized. The navy benevolent fund and the benevolent fund of the air force are fairly wide in their scope, and include service after world war II. The army benevolent fund, on the other hand, as indicated by the hon. member, was set up to deal only with


funds accumulated during world war II. As the minister stated in the house, a benevolent fund is now being established to be known as the Canadian army welfare fund. This will be a continuing fund, will be administered by the same officials and trustees as the army benevolent fund, and will operate in respect to army personnel subsequent to world war II in the same way and under the same conditions generally as the army benevolent fund operates in respect of those who served in the army in world war II. I am not sure if the fund is actually in operation, but if it is not it soon will be.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
At the present time are there not greater privileges for men from the navy and air force than there are for men of the army who served in the second world war? I understand the navy and air force funds are operated by private trustees, whereas the army fund is administered by one of the government departments, and that the soldier is not able to get loans or help of other kinds to the extent it is available to sailors and airmen.
If that is so, the present plan merely stretches out that disadvantage to include the Korean veterans of the army. I should think that from now on Korean army veterans should have exactly the same privileges as are enjoyed by Korean navy and air force veterans.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I might not be correct but I was of the view that the army, navy and air force funds to which we have been referring were administered almost on the same basis. I believe the army benevolent fund is administered under the direction of the army benevolent fund board and that at the present time General Murchie is the chairman of that board. I cannot say categorically that the hon. member is not correct as to there being some difference in methods of application of the three benevolent funds, but I was not aware of it. I shall be glad to look into the matter.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I think the minister will find that there is quite a wide difference. I would ask him to find out, for example, whether a soldier can get a loan from the army benevolent fund. I may not have the correct information but it is my understanding that the army man cannot get a loan whereas the navy man and the air force man can do so from their funds. I also understand that the army benevolent fund is administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Is that correct, or is it not?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I am informed that the hon. member is correct in stating that the army benevolent fund does not make loans, but

the Canadian army welfare fund now being established is being empowered to make such loans. I shall look into the situation.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Is it the intention that the Canadian army welfare fund now being set up will be used to give the army veterans of Korea exactly the same privileges as are enjoyed, and properly so, by naval and air force veterans of Korea?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I understand that is substantially correct.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: What is the procedure with respect to packing plants tendering for the provision of supplies such as meat at army camps? My understanding is that the contracts are given to a select few, and I cannot quite follow the reason for that. I would presume that any licensed packing plant should be permitted to tender, but apparently that is not the procedure. Why is that not so?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: As I mentioned in reply to another question some time ago, the question of tenders for supplies is entirely within the hands of the Department of Defence Production. All we do is requisition what we want. The obtaining of such supplies, whether by tender or otherwise, is in the hands of that department. I am afraid therefore that I cannot answer the hon. member's question as to the basis on which the commodity to which he has referred is obtained.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Then I think it would be a good idea if we left Korea for a while and some of the departments got together. I have a series of letters in my file, and the Department of Defence Production says that it is the Department of National Defence that has the say. The Department of National Defence sent me to the Department of Agriculture, and I expect to land in the Department of National Health and Welfare or maybe external affairs before a concern in the province of British Columbia is able to obtain the opportunity of bidding. I am not suggesting that any particular firm should get a contract but I do insist that any packing plant which is fully licensed by the federal and provincial governments should have the opportunity to bid.
The correspondence does not merely date back a week or two. It runs over a period of months, and if it takes that long for the department to decide among themselves who has the authority, possibly Russia will have declared peace before this concern is able to sell any meat. I am asking for a definite answer. If the minister cannot give it now, then I ask him to have some of his officials- and I understand from the records that there are plenty of officials-check and find out 68108-255
Supply-National Defence why any licensed packing plant in the Dominion of Canada cannot tender on meat supplies particularly for the Department of National Defence. As has been said by someone behind me, Canada Packers and Swift's can get contracts, but Canada Packers, Swift's and Burns should not be the only concerns in the packing line recognized in Canada. If they are, I want to know why they are. Will the minister get me that information?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Order. I allowed the hon. member to put his question and to comment upon the reply, although he received the answer from the minister that tenders are called for by another department. Obviously the minister will give the same reply.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is the first time I have taken part in the debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

In any event, if the minister wishes to comment-

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: All right. I should like to ask another question if I may, which will be in order. Will the minister get for me the names of the packing plants supplying meat to each camp in British Columbia and the amounts of the contracts awarded by each camp within the last fiscal year? Will he also get for me the names of any packing plants in the province of British Columbia which have not been awarded contracts but which have applied? Surely that is in order.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I do not know that it is in order for me to get that information, but I will certainly call the attention of the Department of Defence Production to the inquiry of the hon. member. speechtext:
There is one other matter I should like to place before the associate minister. Press dispatches some weeks ago indicated that Canada is to erect a building in Washington, D.C., for the Canadian joint staff mission. Would the minister tell the committee how much the building, site and

Supply-National Defence equipment are to cost, and also how many people will be occupying the building when it is completed?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister if he will explain why it takes approximately five months for a man being discharged from the service to receive a return of his contributions to the pension fund. This may sound like a small thing but it is not. For example, some of the boys who have returned after spending a year with the 27th brigade in Europe are released from the service after having put in two and a half or three years. When they come out they receive no clothing allowance and, as some of them went into the service at 18 or 20 years of age, they are much bigger when they get out and the clothes they left behind are now no good to them. They need the money to purchase clothing. In correspondence with the department I was told that it takes approximately five months to refund that money. Why should that be? All the documents of the boys are there when they are discharged and the amounts coming to them are known. I think it is unreasonable that they should have to wait that length of time for the return of their contributions. Can the minister explain why it is?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Thank you, sir.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I want to ask the minister about another matter in connection with the
68108-255J
Supply-National Defence 27th brigade in Germany. I am sure the minister and all in his department will have been reading with great interest a series of dispatches from Bill Boss, Canadian Press representative, who has recently gone there. In this particular dispatch, reported in a number of papers, and I am reading from the Ottawa Journal of April 13, in dealing with the difficulties the correspondent states that unit commanders-the three battalion commanders-are experiencing difficulties in connection with the maintenance of regimental traditions and affiliations within their units. The minister will be aware, of course, that when the policy of recruitment of this brigade was announced it was stated that the three infantry battalions-the rifle battalion, the highland regiment and the infantry battalion- would recruit each company from a separate reserve force unit in Canada. That policy was designed to maintain regimental traditions although we on this side said, and I remember that I personally raised the question, that it would in fact make it impossible to preserve regimental tradition. Nevertheless the official answer was that it was felt it would preserve regimental tradition and give each reserve force unit in Canada a spur to recruitment and also an incentive to look after its affiliated company in the corresponding battalion in Germany.
This article reports that cross postings within the battalions from one company to another, which of course are absolutely necessary in the administration of a unit, create enormous difficulties because these men have to take down shoulder patches and, in the case of the highland regiments, they have the wrong kilts, the wrong cap badges and so on. He instances certain cases where complications have arisen as a result of these facts. It is concluded here that the only way to overcome these difficulties is to do what, in fact, we forecast would have to be done, and that is to tell the men to forget that they came originally from the Seaforth or 48th Highlanders or the Royal Regina Rifles, whatever it may be, and tell them that they now belong to simply the First Canadian Highland Regiment or the First Canadian Rifle Regiment, as the case may be.
I want to ask the minister whether, in view of these difficulties which are reported, the department is taking a good look at this system and policy of recruiting, and whether it is not now realized that this system, which was designed to preserve regimental traditions, is in fact having the very opposite effect in making it necessary to tell the men that they can no longer regard themselves as having any affiliation or connection with the

Supply-National Defence parent regiment from which they may have been recruited in Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member has
touched upon a very difficult and serious problem; there is no question about that. The whole matter is, of course, under consideration. I might say that the system of rotation has added to the difficulties the hon. member has enumerated. The principle that was involved when the idea originated is, I think, a good one, and it is sound because it interests every unit across Canada. These difficulties are being studied with a view to seeing what might be done in that connection. The difficulties are great, and the matter is quite complicated, as the hon. member knows.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Does the associate minister not think that ultimately the solution will have to be to name the units over there as entire units, that is if you do desire to maintain regimental traditions and perpetuate that which has been so valuable in infantry formations, that is the regimental spirit? It will be necessary, I believe, to name the units over there by one or other of the reserve force unit names in Canada, that is the whole battalion, instead of trying to keep five separate companies of the five separate regiments. Is it not logical that you will have to arrive at that sooner or later? I want to ask the associate minister whether or not that is the thought in mind, as I hope it will be, rather than that they will simply go on calling it the First Canadian Rifle Regiment or the First Canadian Rifle Battalion, which has no significance or connection with any past Canadian military formations whatever.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I appreciate the views and suggestions of the hon. member, but at this time I would not care to hazard an opinion as to what the ultimate solution will be. I do recognize, as do all the officials of the department, the difficulty to which the hon. member is referring.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether consultations on that question are going forward between the department and the reserve association of the infantry corps, so that their views may be known and considered.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I understand that it will be taken up by the association at its next meeting.

I should like to ask the minister a question or two on the expropriation of land for defence purposes. A constituent of mine in Saskatoon has a lot in Winnipeg, about which I have recently written the minister and I have not yet had time to receive an answer. I make no apology for raising the
IMr. Fulton.]

matter here because I have written once or twice since October, 1952, when the matter was drawn to my attention. I am concerned, of course, particularly in regard to this man's case, but I am concerned also about what I think is the general slackness of the department in attending to either payment or compensation for these various expropriations.
I am referring now to the district in Winnipeg known as the parish of St. James. This lot is in a section close to or adjoining the Carpiquet barracks. There is no necessity for dragging the owner's name into this, but I shall give the minister the number of the lot, lot 18 in block 15, plan 935. This expropriation took place in the year 1941, no less, and is dated December 12. According to a letter which I have, and I think it is over the signature of Mr. Drury, that expropriation was stated to last for the duration of the war and twelve months thereafter. I suggest that many more months have passed since that time. Then, in a letter which I have from the Minister of National Defence himself, dated some time in October, 1952, he said that arrangements have been made now with the city by which this arrangement was to continue until 1956. Well, he mentions arrangements which had been made with the city of Winnipeg, but he did not mention any arrangement made with the owner, and that is exactly the complaint the owner wishes to have brought up in this house.
Then in October, 1952, I have a letter from the assistant deputy minister, one Basil B. Campbell, in which he says to the owner that if the owner will settle on some reasonable price every effort will be made to expedite the transaction. Well, that is fair enough, but so far as I know it has not yet been translated into action.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

If you will make a prompt reply to this letter setting out the price that you wish to receive for the property, the subject will be given careful consideration and if the price is acceptable, every effort will be made to expedite completion of the transaction.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Was there a reply to that letter?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I have no idea as to that, nor have I any idea as to whether or not the lot has been definitely bought. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I am introducing this matter not so much because of this particular case as because I think the whole method is somewhat slack when a man is permitted to go along for 12 years in this state of uncertainty.

I may state that, to my own personal knowledge, a few years ago this man had a definite offer from a potential purchaser. I even knew the price he was offered. He was prevented from making the deal because he could not turn over title to the property. This man is now 74 years of age, and this little bit of property was what he looked upon as his security for his old age. The property has been tied up since 1941 without one cent of compensation being paid. Further, to add insult to what I think is undue injury, this man has had to pay the taxes on the property in the meantime. I can see no justification for that. If that is the system, I think it should be changed quickly. If the government defence department or other departments want to take an option on a piece of land, when the due date for the option comes along, why does not the department take it up or let it go? Why do they not do it by that method and either decide to abandon the property and return it to its rightful owner or pay the agreed price in the terms of the offer?
That is all I have to say in the matter. I hope that this particular case will receive attention. In all fairness to the minister I want to state that the minister has not yet had time-or at least he has not yet found time-to reply to my latest communication and I am looking for that reply in due course. But as I repeat again, I raise the matter in particular to show the general attitude towards expropriations of this nature. I had one close to my own city which had relation to a farm close to Dundurn military camp. We had something of the same sort of trouble about that. I wish to ask the minister to take this matter under his consideration and to let us know what the score is.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am sorry that I am not personally familiar with the case cited by the hon. member but I will undertake to have it looked into at once. I am not personally familiar with the case.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: There is a long file about it.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I wish to ask a question with relation to this large pile of ashes. The only information we have from the minister is that it must have been a large pile. I think we must all agree with that statement. I wonder whether he could produce figures showing the amount of coal that was consumed there to produce this pile and also the price which was paid per ton or per cubic foot to remove these ashes. I ask this question because it seems to be an amount which is out of proportion. Possibly the minister could get those figures and produce them a
Supply-National Defence little bit later, along with the other information he was going to get me with regard to deserters.
While we are on the subject of Petawawa there is another matter which I should like to take up. It concerns the sawmill which was built there and in regard to which I have had three separate questions on the order paper. In answer to one of those sets of questions the minister made a statement at page 2509 of Hansard. The numerous questions elicited information that, during the time that the mill was being operated by the Department of National Defence, lumber was produced to the amount of 1,550,000 board feet, which was valued at $100 per thousand, which makes a value of $155,000. During the first year that this mill was operated, it was operated by day labour, according to the return. During the second year it was operated on contract, at a contract price of $16.30 per thousand. If we assume that the contract price and the day labour price were the same, or approximately so, the cost to cut this amount of 1,550,000 board feet would be $16.30 per thousand multiplied by 1,550, which gives $25,265. The cost of logging in 1949-50 was given as $6,400 and in 1950-51 it is given as $39,999.25. So the cost of logging to provide the logs for this operation was $46,399.25. The total cost of the operation to the department was therefore $71,664.25. To that I would add the cost given for erecting the mill, which was $5,000. Hence the cost to the department of the 1,550 thousand board feet was $76,664.25. They estimated that the value of that was $155,000. Therefore they made a profit on it, or at least they got the lumber for $78,395.75 less than it would have cost them to go out and buy the lumber on the market, according to their own figures.
In spite of that fact, the fact that they got this lumber for less than half of what they valued it at or what they would presumably have had to pay for it on the market, on June 2, 1952, the policy was changed and the
500,000	board feet of lumber which they had on hand and which had cost quite a considerable sum to log off-

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Write them a letter.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
We will not bother going into the exact figures, but the 500,000 board feet which they had already there on hand in the form of logs were sold at $29 a thousand to another firm which presumably has cut or is cutting those logs into lumber. If this amount of 500,000 board feet had been cut into lumber, the cost per thousand for cutting the logs into lumber, according to these figures-$16.30 plus $20 they sold them for-

Supply-National Defence would have been $45.30, a saving of $54.70 from what they could have bought the lumber for. The question which therefore arises is this: Why was the policy changed? If they were getting that lumber for half price, why did they change the policy, sell off these logs at a bargain price and then presumably go ahead and buy lumber at twice what they could have produced it for or more than twice what they could have produced it for? The whole operation just does not seem to make sense. Possibly the answer to the thing is to be found in the answer to one of the questions I put on the order paper about this matter. The question reads as follows:
For what purposes was the lumber, produced at the Department of National Defence sawmill at Petawawa, used, giving the amount used for each project or building.
The answer to that question is a wandering one. It is as follows:
The lumber was used for such things as forms for concrete for the construction of sidewalks, sewers, manholes, etc, the rehabilitation of temporary buildings and temporary married quarters to accommodate the units under training, routine maintenance, summer camp buildings such as shower stalls and field kitchen shelters and other miscellaneous projects, such as targets. Since the lumber used in these projects was drawn from day to day as required over the last four or five years, it would require a great deal of research and analysis to determine the specific quantities used on each particular project.
I just wonder whether all that means is that this large amount of lumber which was produced here they found just dribbled away and they were unable to produce any figures in answer to this question because they did not know what had happened to the lumber; and that possibly the reason that the policy, which seemed to be such a profitable one, was changed was that a great deal of the lumber was lost or had disappeared, and therefore they decided the best thing to do was not to carry on because they were losing the lumber anyway. I should like the minister to answer these questions I have posed and give us some information with regard to this sawmill.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope the hon. gentleman did not expect me to follow his arithmetical calculations throughout as he read them. Generally speaking the situation is this, as I understand it: this operation was carried on by the army for some time, possibly not as efficiently as private industry could carry it on. The fact that it is an unusual industry for the army to engage in, plus the fact that there was a large accumulation of lumber at Petawawa, plus the fact that the price of lumber was falling, all together led to the change in policy which led to closing down of the sawmill at Petawawa.
[Mr. Harkness.l

As to the details which the hon. member has mentioned, I am not going to attempt to deal with them because I did not follow them completely.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: It is not a question of dealing with the details. The question is: When lumber was being produced, according to the figures provided by the department themselves, at half or less than half the cost at which they could have bought it and less than half of what they estimated it was worth, why did they change the policy, and go ahead and sell off the logs they had on hand at a bargain price?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: As I have mentioned, I think the principal reason for a change in policy was that we had a sufficient stockpile of lumber at Petawawa.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The minister says they had a sufficient stockpile for immediate purposes at Petawawa. They are still carrying on building at Petawawa, I believe, and I have no doubt they are using more lumber. They are certainly carrying on building at numerous other places. Why should this lumber, costing them, according to their own figures, less than half what they could have bought it for, have been discontinued?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I would have to check the hon. member's figures. I am not accepting his conclusions, not that I doubt the hon. member's arithmetical capacity, but he has come to a deduction from a long calculation which may or may not be right. I am not admitting his proposition at all.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: These calculations are not long or complicated; they are very short, and they are not over four or five figures. As a matter of fact they are taken directly off the return which the minister supplied himself.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
There are two matters which I wish to receive information about. In the minister's speech on April 14 and in the white paper on page 17 he referred to the regular officers' training plan, R.O.T.P., part of which includes the encouragement given to cadets at the services colleges. Part of that plan includes the fact that from now on service at these services colleges will be pensionable. That is a new departure from what has been the practice in the past. This new departure comes into effect only this year. The result is that there will be certain young officers who have graduated from these services colleges in the army in the future who will be able to count their service at the Royal Military College or Royal Roads, as the case may be, for pension; whereas there will also be young officer graduates of those services

colleges who will not be allowed to count their service for pension. I raised this point during the debate on the speech from the throne before Christmas and asked that consideration be given to permitting all these officers who are graduates of these colleges and who are today serving in the forces to count their time at the services colleges toward pension. May I have a reply to that question, please, because at the time I was told it would receive consideration, and that was several months ago.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The question that my hon. friend refers to involves this consideration, as I understand it. Those who sign on in the services when they enter service college become contributors to the pension scheme, which is a contributory scheme. If their entry into these institutions does not involve that, then they are not eligible for the benefits of the pension scheme. In other words, if they are committed to the service by signing up, they become contributors then and though they are attending these institutions, the time counts. If not, they do not become eligible for the benefits of the pension scheme and do not contribute.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am perfectly aware that it is a contributory pension scheme; but a young graduate from the services colleges now going into the regular army has the privilege of contributing to that pension scheme; but the graduate of last year, before this new plan came in, does not have, as far as I know, the privilege of contributing toward the pension scheme. I am asking that all those who are now serving, whether they graduate four years hence, or whether they graduated last year, be permitted to count their services at the college and make a contribution to cover that time toward their pension scheme. Can that be done?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am informed that that matter has been given study, but up to the present time it has not been deemed advisable to accede to the position that the hon. member takes. I do not know whether it has been finally considered-I would not want to say it has been finally and irrevocably considered-but it has been considered and it has not yet been deemed advisable to do it.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I hope it has not been given final consideration. The injustice and unsatisfactory conditions of having two men serving in the forces under such totally different conditions should be reconsidered.
My other point has to do with the policy in connection with the construction of the permanent quarters. I raised that question
Supply-National Defence in a general way yesterday but I was not satisfied with the answer that I received. Barracks and permanent stations are being built to take care of these forces which we may expect to be permanently stationed in Canada. The information I would like is: Are the plans going ahead to prepare quarters for the airborne brigade so that all the units of the airborne brigade will be closely associated when serving at what one might call their home station, or is the old-fashioned policy, which has been in existence for many years, of building barracks in various parts of the country whereby the units in the same formation did not associate closer together, being continued?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am informed that the airborne brigade referred to by the hon. member as the mobile striking force will not operate as a brigade. It operates as a series of service units stretched across Canada. I believe that the various units which will constitute this mobile striking force will have permanent establishments at different points in Canada.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Can the minister say where the various units will be permanently established? For instance, we have the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, the Royal Canadian Regiment, the Royal 22nd Regiment, the artillery regiments, the Royal Strathcona's Horse and the Royal Canadian Dragoons. Where will the permanent stations of these units be?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I understand that the units of the mobile striking force change from time to time in view of the considerations involved in our other commitments. I do not want to convey the impression that there is a permanent establishment for each given unit. They will be distributed in accordance with the requirements. In other words, the mobile striking force I would say internally rotates similarly to the units abroad.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to make this observation. I was hoping the minister would be able to say that there were permanent quarters for these various regiments. If they are going to be changing from one place to another, then I have this to say. I would call attention to the fact that 40 per cent of the personnel of these units are married, and these constant changes in stations will add a great deal to the expense of maintaining the units, particularly in the matter of married quarters. Again, I think there should be careful consideration as to whether it would not be advisable to allocate to these different units a permanent home.

Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am glad to have the hon. member's views.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I would bring to the attention of the associate minister a matter that has been brought to his attention, and to that of the deputy minister, on previous occasions. I am wondering if anything has been done to protect the member of the permanent force who contributes to the superannuation fund while he is in the service. In the case to which I referred on at least two occasions, the man was in the service ten years before he died, leaving a wife and two children. No pension can be established because the commission has decided his death was not directly attributable to military service, due to the fact that he died from heart failure. The widow is not eligible for war veterans allowance because she is too young.
His contributions made to the pension fund while he was in the service have been returned to her, but the income tax branch has deducted as income tax the sum of $600 from the contribution which was returned. Both the deputy minister and the minister will recall that I raised this matter in the defence committee when we were revising Q.R. (Can.). I brought it to the attention of the committee and said that, at least on the grounds of service loyalty for the benefit of those who had been in the service, some action should be taken as between the Department of Finance and the Department of National Defence.
It is most unfortunate to leave a young woman under those circumstances, and then to add insult to injury by deducting $600 by way of income tax from the contributions made by her late husband. On the occasions I mentioned this matter before, the Minister of Finance indicated that he did not know anything about it. I suggest that, in the interests of those in the permanent service, something should be done to protect those who contribute to the fund and who may run into a similar situation in respect of dependents who are left behind. Has any thinking been done in the matter, and is any action contemplated?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The point the hon. member has raised has been the subject of discussions between this department and the Department of Finance. I cannot tell the hon. member at the moment just what the results have been, or whether the decision has been finalized. However I do recall his observations, and I can say that we have initiated discussions to see what can be done to remedy this situation.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Continue the pressure.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to draw two or three small matters to the


attention of the minister. The first of these has to do with seaward defences. A great deal of damage has been done to the south side wall at the city of St. John's. This matter was discussed before with an official in the department. Has anything been done? The road in question was subject to unusually heavy traffic in the nature of trucks loaded with stone, and the like.
Then I would support the position taken by my colleague the hon. member for St. John's East in connection with the armoury. I know that members of the Canadian army have been looking for an armoury at St. John's. They did inspect a building of which I had knowledge, but for one reason or another they did not find it suitable. I have heard reserve army officers complain about the embarrassment and difficulty they have with the facilities available in connection with the training of men. They say the present accommodation is not suitable, and if we want to have a reserve force down there we should give serious consideration to the question of the armoury. I support that view strongly.
My third question is a much broader one, and has been raised before. It has to do with our troops in Korea. Have they had associated with them at any time any South Korean troops, as has been the case in connection with United States forces? I understand that about a third of the personnel under United States army control are South Koreans. Has the Canadian government given any consideration to the idea of training South Koreans by integrating them with the Canadian forces, or giving them training elsewhere, or by supplying them with arms and other equipment?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
With reference to the hon. member's first question, let me say that negotiations are now going on with the city, and we hope to work out a satisfactory solution so far as the road is concerned. Then I have noted his further representations with regard to the armoury.
In connection with the training of South Koreans, I am informed that steps are being taken in that direction through the commonwealth division, and that we are now waiting for a further report from our own officer commanding in regard to that question.
Then replying to the hon. member for Calgary East, I would say that the contract for the removal of ashes at Petawawa to which he referred also covers refuse generally. The fuel burned at Petawawa amounts to approximately 8,500 tons per year. In addition to other buildings, this includes the heating of 517 permanent married quarters and 415 temporary married quarters.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The minister did not mention the number of tons or cubic yards of ashes removed for this sum of money.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I have not that information.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: If one can judge from the cost of removing the ashes, it would seem there were more tons of ashes than tons of coal burned.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I would have to get the information from the officials of the Department of Defence Production. I do not have it here.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I find here large figures concerning equipment of all kinds. I shall not deal with all of them, but there is one item about which I would ask for the figures because I believe if we had them it might be possible to make useful comparisons. We cannot compare airplanes or tanks with other items, of course; but I would like to have the figures showing the amount spent throughout the whole service on photographic supplies and photographers. I see there are photographers in the army and the navy, but I have not been able to pick out, and I doubt whether the minister can, the amounts showing what has been spent. I want the over-all figure for photographic supplies and persons employed, so that we may have some idea of the total expense in that respect for the services.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I shall be glad to see what can be done about providing the information the hon. member has requested. I might point out that there are many categories; for example, air photography is done for the geodetic survey and guns on our fighters are equipped with cameras. There are all sorts of supplementary forms of photography. I am not sure how we can narrow it down, but we shall do our best to give the information.
While I am on my feet, I should like to put on Hansard the reply to a question raised by the hon. member for Kamloops regarding dismantling buildings at Plouffe park, although I see that he is not in the house at the moment. I am informed that the two buildings to which he referred were temporary shelters erected after the fire there to compensate for some of the storage space that had been lost. These shelters, two large and one small, were of wooden frames with galvanized roofs and tarpaulins over the sides. I understand that the materials cost $12,250 and the labour $6,600 and that the materials are over 90 per cent salvageable. The buildings are now being dismantled because accommodation is becoming available at the new ordnance depot at Cobourg for the stores that have been housed in them throughout the winter.
Supply-National Defence

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Referring specifically to some of the items on page 307, I notice that a number of these items are down considerably from last year, particularly clothing, personal equipment, and barrack, hospital and camp stores. I presume that reflects the fact that mobilization stores of all these items have now all been laid in and that what will be required in future is chiefly what you might call monthly or yearly needs. However, I notice one very large increase in ammunition and bombs, an increase from $38 million to $71 million odd. I should like to ask the same question in connection with this item that I asked with respect to naval ammunition. Does this represent the laying in of mobilization stores or, as in the case of naval ammunition, is it merely ammunition to meet current needs in Korea and for each unit to have a normal stock on hand?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I understand that the
increase will not serve to provide a war reserve but that we are increasing our initial stocks because production is now running fully in many of these items. We are really just completing the accumulation of our necessary permanent stock.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: How much of the heavier calibre gun ammunition is included in that amount? I refer particularly to 25-pounder and/or 105-millimeter and 155-millimeter shells.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: While that information is being sought, might I put on Hansard some observations with respect to the question of the hon. member for Fraser Valley as to how a meat packing plant can qualify to tender. The information I have been given is that in order for a meat packing plant to be eligible for listing with the Department of Defence Production and to receive invitations to tender for the supply of meat and meat products for the Department of National Defence, it must be approved by the dominion Department of Agriculture and is subject to the acts administered by that department. In addition, the prospective tenderer must meet the requirements of Canadian government specifications board, and in order to obtain certification to enable it to tender the packing house must therefore make application to the Department of Agriculture, health of animals division, Ottawa, for plant inspection and approval.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Still on the matter of
ammunition and bombs, can the minister tell us how much of this ammunition is being supplied to our forces in Korea? I think the Minister of National Defence said yesterday that 200,000 rounds of 25-pounder ammunition were supplied in the first year of the Korean war. This amount is not really for war
4038	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence stockpiling. The minister said that all this ammunition really is for current needs and therefore I would think that a considerable proportion of it possibly is going to Korea. Could we find out what amount that is, if any?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I understand that the 200,000 rounds referred to by the hon. member were a contribution we made to the commonwealth pool, but that generally speaking our ammunition, so far as the British type is concerned, is being obtained for Korea at the present time from Great Britain and Australia where some of it is manufactured, and the American type is of course being obtained from the United States. The ammunition covered by the items to which the hon. member referred is mortar ammunition, 60-millimeter, 81-millimeter heavy, ammunition for 90-millimeter anti-aircraft, 105-millimeter howitzer, 105-millimeter recoilless rifle, small arms, ammunition for 3-5 rockets and some other miscellaneous items.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am not clear from the associate minister's answer whether any of the $71 million is for ammunition which will go to our forces in Korea.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: This item does include the cost of ammunition of the various sorts I have mentioned which we will use in Korea.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Can the minister give any indication of what proportion of this total that amounts to?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I understand about 2J per cent, in rough figures.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I understand some is to enable us to build up our initial stock, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, and I think it includes certain tooling in some plants that have to do with new types.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
1 have more than once expressed concern as to the over-all organization of this tremendous enterprise, and I want to draw attention to a few of the departments that I find in the telephone directory of the Department of National Defence. I want to draw attention to the extraordinary division of functions there is now, and then I want to ask a general question. How do we satisfy ourselves that the departments do not become like parallel lines 'Mr. Harkness.]

which, produced ever so far both ways, do not meet? In other words, how is there over-all liaison and inspection and dovetailing of the departments?
First of all let me deal with the directorate of organization which has a personnel of about 30. Then I want to come back and draw attention to some of the departments which are quite heavily staffed. My question again is the broad question of who is responsible, with all the burdens that various people are carrying for their individual work, for saying: This is a good organization; it is functioning as it should, and its relationship is as it should be. I have asked that in the past and I will not take up the time of the committee but I say that there should be fresh outside minds brought into this, even if they are no better than the minds inside.
Having said that, I turn to some of the groups I find here. On pages 11 and 12 I find the inspection service with personnel of about 60. Now, I have no reason to think that is too large.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: To what document is the hon. gentleman referring?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
This is the telephone directory of the Department of National Defence setting out the personnel. On page 13 there is the directorate of civilian personnel, and there are 20 there. On page 15 I find the director of central registries. I am not quite sure what central registries are but there are something like 15 people there. On page 23 I find the director of publications and printing, and there are a dozen or so in that directorate. On page 26-and here you may be getting after me, Mr. Chairman, but it only takes a second to say what I have in mind-I find the directorate of naval information and the directorate of naval intelligence. The directorate of naval information has 9 and the directorate of naval intelligence has 15. I do not know just what the difference between them is.
By anticipation I find a partial answer to my question of a few minutes ago on page 30 I find that there is a superintendent of photography with a staff of about 10. I realize that the question I am asking is a very difficult one to answer, but I feel that it stands out. I feel that when we have this tremendous organization we should in some way be satisfied that people skilled in that sort of thing are used to vet this organization. The most gallant officer in the world, the best man in the field, the man you would choose above all others to command men going into action, may not be good at organization. My own belief is that a man,

unless he is a genius, has to learn organization as he has to learn anything else. I throw that question out and leave it to the minister to answer as best he can, and I believe it is an important question.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: May I just make this general observation, Mr. Chairman, on the point raised by the hon. member, which I am sure he does not expect me to develop in detail. These different branches have been set up for specific purposes. For example, in the inspection service there is a controller of inspection who is responsible for the activities of that branch. These branches have been correlated and knit together as time has passed. In addition, there is the director of organization of the civil service commission who, in the Department of National Defence as in every other department, is continually making surveys along the lines of the observations of the hon. member and bringing to our attention suggestions for improvement and change. There is also the treasury office which, just the same as in other departments, is constantly making suggestions and reviewing the operations of these phases of the department. The fact that the department is large is occasioned, of course, by the magnitude of the things it is endeavouring to do. I do feel from my short association with the Department of National Defence that the different groups are co-ordinated and are under continual surveillance so that the standard of efficiency that is being developed is high and compares very well with other departments. Beyond that I do not know that I should make any detailed comment at the moment.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I am not
going to labour the matter, but I just make this point. We have something here that is as far as the east is from the west from the situation in an ordinary department by reason of (a) its magnitude, and (b) the rapidity with which it has to be developed. I realize, as I said before, that I cannot ask the minister to give me a detailed statement of how these things fit, but I shall reiterate what I said before. I think the situation cries out for the best outside brains that can be brought in to assist. That is not without precedent in this government, as I understand it was done in one quite small department. At the risk of being tiresome I am going to reiterate that it should be done, unless there are reviews going on that I know nothing about and of which we have not been told.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Shall we pass on to air force?
68108-256i
Supply-National Defence

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: No. In referring to the details on page 307, I notice an amount of $17 million odd this year for tanks and armoured fighting vehicles. Last year it was $22 million. I wonder if the minister can tell us how many up to date tanks, Centurion tanks, we secured last year and how many more it is expected we are going to get. Also, what other items might be covered by this particular expenditure in addition to the Centurion tanks.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I think the hon. member will appreciate why I do not wish to give the figure in regard to tanks either for stocks or anticipated purchases. I think they have not been given at any place or at any time, and probably it is not desirable to do so.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I might just say that at this time last year the Minister of National Defence gave the number of Centurion tanks we had purchased up to that time. I have forgotten it exactly, but it was a small number and it was given.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister agree to say whether or not the two permanent active force regiments, Lord Strathcona's Horse and the R.C.D.'s, are going to be equipped with Centurion tanks?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The answer is yes.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Before we pass from the army to the air force I want to ask one question regarding the northwest highway system which is allocated under army. Are any funds placed under the heading of the northwest highway system allocated to that portion of the system known as Haines cut-off?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The appropriations for the northwest highway system includes an appropriation for that.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Is there any intention to keep Haines cut-off open all year round in the future? In the past it has only been kept open during the summer months.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I am informed that this particular phase of the highway system is a joint operation by Canada and the United States. At the present time it is intended to continue keeping it open throughout the summer season only.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Can you tell us how much was spent on the Haines cut-off last year? I know it is a joint operation between ourselves and the United States, but from the point of view of national defence it can hardly be considered a contribution to the defence of northern Canada, although I realize it is a very considerable contribution to the defence of Alaska.

Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I will have to get that figure for the hon. member and I shall do so. I have not got it with me.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The reason I am asking this question is that it must be realized that if we are spending a great deal of money on this Haines cut-off, it will be in direct competition with the White Pass and Yukon Railway which runs through Canada, and which operates on a very narrow margin. If considerable traffic is going to be trucked over the Haines cut-off it will affect the interests of the railway.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Reverting to this matter of the armoured fighting vehicles, the minister told us that two reserve force armoured units are being equipped with Centurion tanks.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Those are regular force units.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Did I say reserve? I am sorry; I meant to say regular force units. My question is, are the reserve force armoured units to be equipped with these Centurion tanks also?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: We are endeavouring to complete arrangements to provide for the training of reserve forces on Centurion tanks.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I am glad to know that the reserve units are going to get some Centurion tanks for training purposes. I hope they will get them at an early date.
There is an item for mechanical equipment, including transport, which is up from $30 million to $33 million. In the defence expenditure committee last year we received details concerning a number of vehicles which had been ordered at that time. When we were dealing with the matter at that time very few of these vehicles had been delivered. I wonder if the minister could tell us how the deliveries of these vehicles have been, and whether the vehicles on order at that time are now in the hands of defence forces.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I can get the details if the hon. member wants them, but I can say that very substantial progress is being made. If my recollection serves me correctly I think one type is completed, and they are all very close to being completed.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Those are the ones with which we were dealing in the committee last year?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Then this $33 million represents the sum available for more vehicles of the same sort; is that correct?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The next item is armament equipment, which would be guns and so forth. It is merely $23 million this year and was $17 million last year. Last year the minister said very good progress had been made toward beginning to produce 105- and 155-millimeter cannon in Canada. I wonder if he can give us a progress report on that and let us know to what extent that type of equipment is being substituted for the 25-pounders and 4-5's and 5-5's which were used within the last year or two.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: We are still making good progress with the 105 and 155's. We have an order for our own account as well as that of the United States under production.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Would the minister care to give any figures on the production of those?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: There are no deliveries yet, except of what might be called tool room or prototype models.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The minister says we have not yet got into production?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: They are producing, but we have not had deliveries yet.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Then this item of $23 million covers chiefly cannon and things of that sort, or is there any appreciable portion of that for small arms? If so, what type of small arms would it cover?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: A large amount, more than $15 million, is for Are control equipment in the 90 millimeter ack-ack guns to which I referred before. It can be understood that that is very expensive equipment. For engineering, bridging, boats and so on, there is about $12 million; field artillery equipment of various types, $10 million; small arms, mortars, $4 million; maintenance, spare parts, ancillary, $8 million; that is a total of $50 million.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Excuse me, but where does the minister get this $50 million? That must be the expenditure for the past two or three years.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: That is the commitment authority and forward program. The actual cash to be spent out of that is $22,950,000 but it is not allocated, because how much cash is spent on each item will depend on the progress we can make.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: In connection with the $4 million which is for small arms-

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Yes, but none of it is for rifles.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I was just going to ask what type of small arms was meant.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Almost entirely for mortars of new types.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I was going to ask particularly if anything had been done in regard to submachine guns. I had a question on the order paper back in February as to what type of submachine gun was issued to Canadian troops in Korea. I asked if this type of submachine gun was found satisfactory in action, and if not, what were the deficiencies. Has a different type of submachine gun been issued? The answer I received at that time was that the carbine machine Sten 9 mm. Mk. 2 was being used. It was stated that, while not entirely satisfactory, it is regarded as being as satisfactory as other available types. It has certain disadvantages, particularly in the magazine. I was informed that a different type of submachine gun had not been issued for operational use, but a more recent type has been issued for user trials.
I wonder if any progress has been made in arming the entire brigade with this new and, I would take it, more satisfactory type of submachine gun?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: There is not yet, that I am aware, a better submachine gun than the ones we have. We are subjecting both a British type and an American type to trials at the present time. The Bren gun is still a very satisfactory weapon.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Could the minister say what is this more recent type which has been issued for user trials, and what have been the results of those trials?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
I would have to get some technical details on that. I am not in a position to give very much information. We are in the hands of our friends the Americans and the British who designed the weapons, and we could not give very much information on the results without their concurrence.
I have one answer that I wanted to give to the hon. member for Nanaimo. He asked the principle upon which married accommodation was being provided for the active forces. We have made an actual count of the number of people in the active forces as presently constituted, and arrived at an exact figure for all for whom accommodation is to be provided in the program. It has not yet been provided, but we are working toward it, and the figure is just over 25,000.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before passing on to the next item I notice that there is an item on pages 309 and 310 relating to the northwest
Supply-National Defence highway system, amounting to nearly $9 million. I take it that refers to the highway from Edmonton through to Alaska. If so may I again avail myself of this opportunity of suggesting that the department add to that highway the portion of No. 5 highway running from Edmonton to Winnipeg. We have been discussing this afternoon many of the various kinds of mobile units, not that we hope we shall have to use them in our own country, but a time might come when we would be glad to roll them from the east to the northwest. I think consideration should be given to the inclusion of No. 5 highway from Winnipeg to Edmonton, leaving Winnipeg and going through Saskatoon, North Battleford, Battle-ford, Lloydminster and on to Edmonton. I would suggest to the minister that this proposal still be given serious consideration.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for The Battlefords and other hon. members have drawn this matter to the attention of the government on a number of occasions. It came up for consideration during the course of the discussion on the estimates last year. In addition, representations have been received from the governments of the three prairie provinces.
I am afraid I must say there is little likelihood of the federal government or the Department of National Defence ever reaching that satisfactory position with regard to its defences-equipment, construction, manpower and everything else-where it would be able to engage in such an activity as the grading, from the defence point of view, of a highway for which the provinces should ordinarily be responsible. Everything which adds to our communications or transportation system is, of course, of some benefit in defence. But having said that, I must say there are so many more things that we cannot afford to buy and do not expect to be able to afford to buy for our defence and which are more urgently required, that the highway is fairly low in priority.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister tell the committee the present situation with regard to the Canadian Rangers? speechtext:

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: How many units are in being? The minister said that 1,500 men are enrolled.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I would have to get that information.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: In what part of the country are they located?

speechtext: Very largely in the western part of the Arctic, west of Hudson bay out to the Pacific coast. There are some east of Hudson bay, but very few.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: The minister will get the number for me?

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Yes. I shall be glad to give that information to the hon. member.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I have just one further question which I think might come here. I want information with regard to contracts where the plans and specifications have been amended in the course of a contract and where that has inevitably involved additional expenditure. I am quite ready to accept a suggestion as to a floor, so to speak; but I should like to get information as to the important cases where that has happened.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

speechtext:
If I may
interrupt, I want to make it clear that I am willing to accept a reasonable floor so we will not run into useless work.

speechtext: Even with a reasonable floor you would get hundreds or thousands.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:

suppose we will run into thousands that have been amended.
