speechtext:
No; but in order to find out whether or not it is amended you have to look at it; and this would mean an examination of individual contracts through the Department of Defence Production and its agencies, Defence Construction Limited and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I would think that in a considerable number


of contracts there had been additions and amendments made in the course of the construction which had led to additional expense. We would be glad to arrange for that information to be worked out and put before the defence expenditure committee, if it was desired.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
No, it is not
carried. I am informed that there is a question as to the amount of work involved.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I have given the hon. member the information I have. maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext: I myself was going to make that suggestion. If that is satisfactory to the minister we will leave it there. I should like to add that I like to think I am fairly reasonable, and I think we can work out something so there will not be a whole lot of useless clerical work to do.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
This is a proposal that merits some comment. This afternoon the associate minister said that this Canadian joint staff mission building in Washington was to cost $2 million. He now says that the site has cost $115,000 and the rentals being paid for the present accommodation amount to $47,488. This appears to me to be another instance of money being wasted, of Canada trying to live up to the Joneses in the matter of buildings beyond our country's boundaries, and a very unfair burden on the taxpayers of the country. The press dispatch which first announced this building was dated December 29, 1952. I am reading from the Vancouver Province:
Canada has purchased a site here for a new $1 million building to house the Canadian joint staff mission, the Evening Star says.

Supply-National Defence
Hon. members will notice that the cost of that building has now gone from $1 million to $2 million. Then the dispatch goes on:
The property involved now occupied by a fraternity house is in a fashionable area on Massachusetts avenue. It is several blocks from the British and Canadian embassies.
I cannot see the reason for the construction of a $2 million building for a Canadian joint staff mission in a fashionable area in Washington. It is about time the government got back to the old Canadian virtue of thrift. Here we have a situation which will not be permanent. For the time being 228 Canadians will be housed in that building. I presume that they will all be living elsewhere, and living accommodation will have to be provided in addition. It will only be a matter of time until that joint staff mission will be greatly reduced. Surely here is one place where we could get a building for a good deal less than $2 million. I take it that the building has not yet been constructed, and therefore that it is not too late for the department to give some further consideration to its cost.
A similar situation arose in the committee on external affairs with regard to an embassy in Italy. The tentative plans called for an embassy which, with equipment, would cost over $1 million. As a result of the complaints made in the committee the Department of External Affairs is to review the plans in an effort to cut down the expenditure. I would hope that the same plan will be followed by the Department of National Defence with regard to this joint staff mission building in Washington. I do not believe the Canadian people should be saddled with an expense of $2 million for a building of that kind.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT MEASURE PROVIDING FOR ORGANIZATION AND SUPERVISION OF ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member has made some observations which of necessity were made without knowledge of the facts. Almost without exception, Washington is the most difficult place to get accommodation in that we know of. The joint staff mission is now located in two buildings on Massachusetts avenue, but they are the property of the Australian government. We succeeded in getting the leases to them at a time when space was not quite so tight and because we were a friendly government engaged in the same kind of operation. It was a fair lease, but the buildings are by no means suitable for the purposes for which they are used. Nevertheless we would like to stay there but unfortunately we are being put out in October of this year. I myself have appealed to the Prime Minister of Australia to let us stay on for another year; otherwise we will have


to house this joint staff in temporary accommodation, probably in a hotel or an apartment house at terrible expense.
We searched the city of Washington for any building that could be used for this purpose. We had the leading real estate agents in Washington conduct that search for us. We had representatives of the Department of Public Works and the Department of External Affairs work with us to try to find any type of building. We did not want to build, and we just could not find anything suitable. If the hon. member knows of a better place in Washington we would be glad to take it, but I do not believe there is such a place.
As for the land, we got it at a very favourable price. It is between $2 and $3 a foot which, as the hon. member knows, is a very favourable rate indeed for land in any large city, and particularly a city like Washington where prices are very high.
If it should turn out that we can reduce our joint staff there, then the building is sufficiently close to our embassy to enable it to be used as an annex of the embassy. That is one useful thing about this location. However, our experience is that in the case of relations with countries like the United Kingdom and the United States the extent of governmental business, whether it be defence or otherwise, has tended to increase; thus it appears we will always have the need for this place, either for civilian or service purposes. As I say, the location happens to be convenient to the embassy. But the land at between $2 and $3 a foot is a very good purchase, and at a very low cost. We could not find anything comparable in any suitable area in Washington.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Thatcher for the second reading of Bill No. 108, to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to think that when this bill was first introduced exception might have been taken to it, by way of a point of order, that it touched upon a subject matter already covered by another bill

then before the house and which had been forecast in the speech from the throne, namely a bill to consolidate the Criminal Code. In any case, as it happens we are at the present time debating this subject of capital punishment on the bill before us in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), and at the same time a House of Commons committee is discussing the identical subject as one of the sections of the Criminal Code bill.
I do think, with all deference-and in this I believe I express views with which those who have taken part in the debate would agree-that the question as to whether or not capital punishment should be retained is one of great importance, complexity and difficulty, and perhaps is deserving of somewhat more profound attention than has been given it in the debates which have taken place almost every year in this chamber.
For example, we have the argument as set out in the Mosaic law: Thou shalt not kill. And in the very next chapter of Exodus, the book of the Bible in which that occurs, we have set out, as related to that statement of a crime, the punishment for that crime, where in the 12th verse it says:
He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death.
And in the 15th and 16th verses:
And he that smiteth his father, or his mother, shall be surely put to death.
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
So when we make this quotation, and it is a very common quotation, against capital punishment, as it is set out in the Mosaic law- and I am not adopting it for the purpose of any argument I am advancing-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: There is such a thing as the New Testament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
I quite agree; but it is the Old Testament which is quoted. The injunction "Thou shalt not kill", which is the definition of a crime, is suggested as a reason why capital punishment should not be inflicted, whereas just a few lines farther on in the same chapter, and from the same authority, the suggestion is made that capital punishment is a punishment suitable for the crime so defined. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said there is such a thing as the New Testament, and of course I entirely agree with him. I agree also with what I take it he implied, and that is that the New Testament might adopt a different attitude toward capital punishment.
Criminal Code
May I, as having some bearing upon what the hon. member has in mind, refer him to the contribution made by the present Archbishop of Canterbury, as it is set out in the parliamentary debates in England for 1947 and 1948, where he makes this statement:
The statesman-even the Christian statesman- has to deal with society as it is at any given moment; and though he be guided and impelled by Christian doctrine and ethics, he will have to decide constantly how far, in the fulfilment of his trust as the guardian of society, he must rely on preventive and deterrent methods of punishment only and how far he can mitigate them and make them constructive by the operation of the law of love. It is the same question which every citizen and every Christian has to consider, and it has to be decided by each man according to his own judgment, discrimination and experience.
The church, in its corporate capacity, does not pronounce in such a matter. Each Christian has the duty of conscientious private judgment, and Christians very naturally and rightly differ in their estimate of what is practicable.
Then he makes this further observation:
The duty of the state is to protect society against this horrible crime. There is, shall I say, a prima facie case for the law of the state to inflict the death penalty upon one who takes the life of another. It goes to the self-preservation of society. The state must begin by asking, not what is for the good of the murderer-that must come second *-but what is necessary for the good order of society, life and the safety of its citizens.
I think as good a statement as can be found as to the relationship between jurisprudence, or the law at large, and the question of capital punishment, is that contained in the ninth edition of Jurisprudence, by the late Sir John Salmond. This is the classical statement on the subject and it states:
The ends of criminal justice are four in number, and in respect of the purposes so served by it, punishment may be distinguished as, (1) deterrent, (2) preventive, (3) reformative, and (4) retributive. Of these aspects, the first is the essential and allimportant one-*
That is, the deterrent.
-the others being merely accessory. Punishment is before all things deterrent, and the chief end of the law of crime is to make the evildoer an example and' a warning to all that are like-minded with him.
Thus the prime object of criminal law is, in the words of the great English political philosopher, Locke, to make every offence very obviously a bad bargain for the offender. After the deterrent aspect is placed preventive punishment, for we are not concerned merely with deterring offenders but also with preventing them from repeating the offence by such penalties as imprisonment or, in capital cases, death.
Sir John Salmond in that connection makes what seems to me a very profound observation, although it is a short one. He says, "Offences are committed through the

Criminal Code
influence of motives upon character" and thus "may be prevented either by change of motives or by a change of character. Punishment as deterrent acts in the former method; punishment as reformative in the latter". It is clear, he concludes, "that there is a necessary conflict between the deterrent and the reformative theories of punishment". And it is necessary, in view of modern tendencies, "to insist on the primary importance of the deterrent element in criminal justice". He puts it this way:
The reformative element must not be overlooked, but neither must it be allowed to assume undue prominence. To what extent it may be permitted in particular instances to overrule the requirement of a strictly deterrent theory is a question of time, place and circumstances.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, if I were to cite, as I could cite, for example, the records of the six states of the United States of America in which capital punishment has been abolished and which show that their rate of murder, according to the figures I have here, is something of the order of three times as high as it is in Canada, or if I were to cite the fact that during the interval between when New Zealand abolished capital punishment in 1941 and restored it in 1950 their rate of homicide was several times higher than in Canada, I would not suggest for a moment that these statistics necessarily have any great force or relevancy as applied to the problem before us.
I say that because we know that one of the most elementary rules of logic is that if you are going to compare two separate countries statistically in that way you first have to be able to say that the only factors which differ as between the two you are comparing are whether they have capital punishment in one case and no capital punishment in the other, and that all the other factors which might influence the rate of homicide are identical in the two countries.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: How do their own rates compare before and after?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: I could not say. I have just compared during the period.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Does the minister know how the rates in these six states compare with those in other states?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Again I suggest to my hon. friend that there are numerous factors which might account for the difference. Therefore, if we are making a serious attempt at thinking our way to a proper solution of the problem, I do not really believe it serves any purpose for those who favour the retention of capital punishment to cite the case of the six American states or of New Zealand, or 
that it serves any purpose for those who favour the abolition of capital punishment to cite the experience of the Scandinavian states where you have a very high homogeneity of population speaking the same language in each case, largely of the same religion, having the same outlook upon life and with no frontiers in the sense in which we have one on the North American continent.
Therefore if we are going to do any useful thinking in this field we have to get above the matter of basing it upon newspaper clippings and casual statistics of the very sort to which I have just been referring generally myself. That is why I think, if I may be permitted to transgress slightly in view of the fact that we are discussing a matter which I suggest should not be before the house at all, that perhaps the best method of dealing with it is the one that was suggested in the special committee on the Criminal Code the other day, namely that when we have accomplished the really monumental task to which we are now addressing ourselves, the consolidation of no less than 60 odd years of amendments to the code into one entity, we might then either set up a parliamentary committee or a royal commission for the express purpose of considering such matters as capital punishment or the rule of legal insanity, as in the M'Naughton case, and other major problems of that character.
It was suggested that along with the resolution reporting the Criminal Code bill back to the house a recommendation might be made that, while the committee had not considered these major matters and did not think it appropriate to do so in conjunction with another very large and complex task, the government and the house at a later date might either set up a parliamentary committee or a royal commission to consider matters of that sort. I think there will be general agreement not only by those who have taken part in the debate this year and in similar debates of previous years but by every member of the house that in the question of the retention of capital punishment we have a very large, difficult and complex problem, and we are not living up to our responsibilities if we consider it in any other light.
Before we reach any conclusions we have to get beyond newspaper clipping logic and consider the matter carefully over a period of time, hear competent people who are for it and competent people who are against it and then, having gathered a mass of reliable data, reach our conclusions and apply our

own reasoning to that data in order to bring about, if it is thought advisable, a change in the law; or, if it is not thought advisable, to have a much better informed opinion ourselves and a much better informed public opinion upon the subject.
For that reason, if I might be permitted to do so, I should like to suggest to my hon. friend that he might consider withdrawing the bill and leaving the matter to be dealt with by the parliamentary committee which has a bill before it upon this same subject which is in order and which they are considering in the manner in which I have indicated.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question. He gave us certain statistics and information regarding states and countries which have abolished capital punishment. Has the minister figures showing not a comparison of their rate with Canada's so far as homicide is concerned, but showing their rate of homicide while they had capital punishment and the rate after they abolished it? I think he would then be comparing something under circumstances which are similar.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: No, I have not. The restoration of capital punishment in the case of New Zealand was in 1950, and the time lag with respect to the securing of these statistics is such that I doubt very much if any reliable statistics are available. Then, as I am sure my hon. friend will agree, statistics of this sort, which are not plentiful in any country, are only reliable, it would seem to me, if they are examined over a fair period of time.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill. I am constrained to do so as much by what the minister has proposed as by my support of the bill of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher).
I am opposed to capital punishment and I am supporting the bill. I think, whether we agree with the purposes of the bill or not, that the member for Moose Jaw should be commended for bringing it before the house. I appreciate that it is a question upon which there is very wide difference of view, but I believe an ever-increasing number of people are coming to realize that capital punishment is not only ineffectual as a deterrent to homicide but it also has other psychological effects that are not beneficial to society. I think the penalty of "a life for a life" which we now carry out with capital punishment was an act of revenge in other and more primitive days. Civilized society everywhere is getting away from the old idea of revenge
Criminal Code
and taking the much broader view, as the minister said, of protecting society.
A little while ago I read somewhere a statement made by a retired officer of the metropolitan police in London. After many years of experience in dealing with crime he gave it as his opinion that the difference between the state of mind that resulted in crime and the normal state of mind was very, very narrow indeed; and that no one could say when he would be himself in an emotional state where a crime of violence would seem to be the natural thing to do. If that is the case, the person who commits murder is not in any normal state of mind; and whether he is insane or knows what he is doing is not a question of great importance. I think we will agree that such a person really has not much control over his actions, and for that reason I think it would be much better to protect society by seeing that he is not allowed to mix with society again than by going through the very brutal proceedings by the infliction of capital punishment. I think the method we use in carrying out capital punishment is the most revolting of any being used at this time.
The suggestion made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is a good one, even though the member for Moose Jaw may not agree. I do not know whether he will agree, though I imagine he will because it is a reasonable suggestion. If the hon. member does not agree the likely result in connection with this bill would be that it would go to a vote and be defeated in the house, and that would be the end of it for this year. However, if the committee on criminal law should bring a recommendation to the house concerning capital punishment, and the other things the Minister of Justice referred to, to the effect that they should be dealt with by a royal commission or a parliamentary committee, then I would think the member for Moose Jaw had made some progress by the introduction of his bill.
I do not think there is anything further I need to say; but if my advice is of any value to the hon. member, I would suggest that withdrawing the bill in view of what has been said by the Minister of Justice would be the proper course at this time.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on this bill which has been presented to the house by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). I am not a lawyer and I cannot talk about the legal aspects of the bill, but I do believe the bill has considerable merit in it. I think the abolition of capital punishment is something we might well consider in this day and age. I think, too,

Criminal Code
that we have considered bills in this house which have had much less merit than this present bill.
I am not too greatly concerned about how a criminal is put to death. I do not think it makes a great deal of difference to one who is going to lose his life whether he is to be guillotined, hanged or sent to the electric chair. 1 understand that in France they still use the guillotine. In Great Britain individuals are hanged for the offence of murder, and in this country we follow that same procedure. In the United States the electric chair is generally used.
My concern in regard to capital punishment is for the immediate friends and relatives of those who are to be hanged. It seems to me that hanging is a pretty cruel death; but again I say that I do not think it makes too much difference to the man who is going to be hanged just what happens to him. He has been found guilty in the courtroom and the judge has said that he will be hanged until he is dead. I do not think the method makes too much difference to the criminal, but I do have in mind possibly parents, a brother or sister or close relatives and friends of that criminal, and I think the effect on them is very important.
The minister has suggested that this matter may be referred to the committee on criminal law and I think in this day and age it is time we looked into capital punishment and, if we are going to continue to have it in this country, see if there might not be a better method. I repeat that my concern is for those who are close relatives of the one who is to be hanged. I have a family, and it seems to me that if one of my sons got into trouble and had to pay that penalty under the law of the country, then it would be some consolation to me, if capital punishment could not be abolished, if we had a more humanitarian way of taking the life of that individual. My hon. friend in front of me says I may be hanged myself, but I will take that chance. In the United States they use the electric chair, and I think that is a more humane way for one to be put to death.
That is all I am going to say and I suppose that the hon. member for Moose Jaw will withdraw his bill. However, if it goes to a vote I will support it.

Mr. Speaker, I merely want to say that I support the bill, and I congratulate the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) for having brought this matter to the attention of the house as he has done year after year. I tried to follow the minister's argument to discover whether or not he was in favour of capital punishment. I think everyone reading his remarks will find it rather difficult to conclude which way the minister was arguing. I would gather, however, that the minister is not prepared at this time to support the bill.
If the minister is not prepared to support it, and if he is speaking for the cabinet, then of course the bill has not a chance in the world of passing the house. The only recourse open to the hon. member is to follow

the minister's suggestion, unless he wants to see the bill defeated by an overwhelming majority.
I think there is a growing number of people throughout this country who are opposed to capital punishment. The committee which is revising the Criminal Code has had a number of representations made to it expressing that opinion, and a number have asked that a commission be set up this session in order to study the question of abolishing capital punishment and abolishing whipping. I am pleased to gather from the minister's remarks, whether or not he is in favour of abolishing capital punishment, that he will support a resolution coming from that committee recommending the setting up of a parliamentary committee to study this matter at some length. In the light of that fact I shall support the withdrawal of this bill, if it is withdrawn. If it is not, I shall vote in favour of it.

If you want to prevent crime, as I view it-and I have talked to much wiser people than I shall ever be-and from what I have read, the only way to prevent a crime of this nature is by humiliation. Hanging not only extinguishes the life of the chief felon, but it also imposes a very severe punishment on the family of the felon.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege because it is a matter which is of some concern to several

Supply-National Defence members of the house. We have had a long and heavy week, and so far we have sat every evening. The page boys have been kept extremely busy. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Do I understand that we have disposed of the subheading "Army"?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, while the house was considering private bills I had an opportunity to check up on the reports of the earlier discussion. The associate minister was to get me further information with regard to this army benevolent fund. In his earlier remarks he did not make it clear whether the Korean army veteran will now be able to get loans and have all the privileges which are enjoyed by a Korean navy veteran and a Korean air force veteran. As the associate minister will remember, he was uncertain of the situation at that time. I would ask for a further explanation now.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: To reply to the hon. member's further question, it is my understanding that under the new fund to which I referred and which will be applicable to the Korean veterans of the army, called the Canadian army welfare fund, they will be permitted to obtain loans and generally speaking-I cannot say in every specific detail-the purview of this new fund will be similar to that of the navy benevolent fund and the air force benevolent fund. These are private funds, as the hon. member will understand; they are not government funds. They are administered in trust. I am told that the general field covered by the new Canadian army welfare fund, together with the benevolent fund, will be parallel to the other two.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Will the funds be administered by the same board which administers the army funds from the second great war?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes. I understand that
the administration will be carried on by the same agency that administers the army benevolent fund.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Then the veteran of the
second world war will not have the same rights as the veteran of the Korean war? Will that be the position? In other words, this army board will be administering two different funds in different ways. There will be more privileges pertaining to the fund which is now being set up for the Korean army veteran.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The hon. member is correct. Unless and until the army benevolent fund is changed, it has a limitation which does not obtain in respect of either the naval benevolent fund or the air force benevolent fund or the new Canadian army welfare fund which will be available to the veterans from Korea.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
When will that fund be
set up?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is in the process of being set up now. I think the organization part is practically completed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Shall the subheading carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speechtext:
We shall then
proceed to the subheading "Royal Canadian Air Force-Regular and General", found at page 311 of the blue book.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
On the subject of the air
force there are several questions I should like to raise, and I think I will present the whole group of questions while I am on my feet, if I may. During the minister's remarks on April 14 he had this to say as reported at page 3811 of Hansard:
During 1952-53 there were 19 regular airfields, stations and schools opened bringing the total number used by the air force up to 108. Another 13 regular and 7 auxiliary schools and stations will be opened during 1953-54.
That statement indicates that an expansion of air force training facilities is contemplated for the current fiscal year. I should like to ask the associate minister whether he could give further details as to the expansion contemplated. For example, would it be possible to indicate where and when these 13 regular and 7 auxiliary schools are going to be located?
Continuing along that same line dealing with the expansion of auxiliary schools, I do not know whether that refers to reserve training or not, but in the estimates I notice that the expenditure for auxiliary operations is decreasing from $5,718,162 to a figure of $5,286,200 for the forthcoming fiscal year. I should like to discover the reason for the decrease. That would tend to indicate that

no further expansion in the auxiliary operations is contemplated, something which seems to be contrary to the statement I have read from page 3811 of Hansard.
If the auxiliary operations are to be extended, if there is to be an expansion of the number of auxiliary squadrons, I should like to remind the associate minister that for some two or three years now the air force association in the city of Brandon has been very interested in participating in this form of reserve activity. They are a very keen group; at the present time they are not tied to any active program of reserve training. They have won a pennant award for their participation in association activities this year, and they would be interested in any expansion of reserve activities of this nature that might be undertaken.
That brings me to the mobilization assignment training program. I am getting all sorts of information these days about defence matters in general and air force matters in particular. This morning in my mail a circular letter reached my desk. It is the first issue of what is called the M.A.T.P. officers' training school. I believe they are going to circulate a monthly information sheet of this kind. As I read this circular it would seem to me it is expected that there will be some expansion in this form of reserve training. On page 2 of the circular it is indicated that the first course for mobilization air training personnel is to get under way in September of this year, a course in flying control activities. It is hoped that circumstances will soon permit additional courses for personnel engaged in other types of employment. That seems to deal with one of the complaints I made the other day to the effect that reserve people having a special background of training are not being fitted into the area of service for which they are most suitably prepared.
I should like to commend the department for its activity in this regard. A list of the personnel already participating in the M.A.T.P. is attached, and the implication I get from this list is to the effect that more and more reserve people are to be absorbed in this type of training program. I think it is a very worthy activity. If the minister has anything further to say on this matter I would appreciate having it.
Finally, coming back to the association problems again, I am wondering just what form of assistance is available to air force association wings across the country. It is a veterans' group that is officially recognized by the R.C.A.F. and the Department of National Defence. Up to the present time most of its activities have been of a social
Supply-National Defence nature, but they are trying to contribute in some more concrete way. I know that our own wing, the 502 wing, has recently established a club and they are interested in knowing whether any assistance is available in the form of furnishings and that sort of thing that could be used in equipping a mess. At the present time we have not been able to get any concrete information in that regard. That covers most of the questions I had in mind.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
With reference to the first question asked by the hon. member for Brandon, I have not a list of the 13 regular and 7 auxiliary schools and stations that are referred to on page 3811 of Hansard, but I would observe first that these figures include major Royal Canadian Air Force formations and units, including wing headquarters, ground and operational units, supply depots and radar units as well as actual flying units.
With respect to the auxiliary units, I can give the hon. member the location of the 7: Saskatoon, 2; Calgary, 2; Saint John, New Brunswick; Windsor, Ontario; London.
On the second point as to the apparent decrease in the air force estimates, I am told that the discrepancy to which the hon. member referred was owing to the fact that there was an overprovision in the estimates of last year. It is not owing to an actual decrease in the activity.
With regard to the air force association, it is my understanding that a grant of $15,000 a year is given to the association and the members are given a free subscription to the Roundel; but no other assistance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I take it that no movement is under way to increase the number of auxiliary squadrons in operation in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Not flying.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Not flying squadrons?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No.
