Supply-Trade and Commerce years I have used this opportunity to make a statement about economic conditions in Canada and about the efforts being made by the Department of Trade and Commerce to maintain and expand Canada's trade with the outside world. To some extent both have already been covered by my colleague the. Minister of Finance, in his budget speech; and during the budget debate I gave an account of my trip to Latin America.
It seems to me that hon. members should have before them when they consider the estimates of my department a brief account of what has been happening under the economic and trade policies followed by the government. The simplest way I can describe the present economic situation in Canada is to say that at no time in the past have Canadians been more prosperous. In spite of the predictions of recessions and depressions that were made from time to time the fact is that the pace of Canadian production has rarely faltered since the end of the war. Our country has attracted the attention of the world because of its economic stability and rapid development.
Of course it has not all been smooth sailing. There have been times when shortage of key materials interfered with the attainment of maximum output. There have been times when loss of external markets caused distress to some producers. But in the end most of these difficulties proved to be limited in their scope or of relatively short duration. New records of national output were attained from year to year.
At the beginning of 1952, for example, there were many uncertainties. On the one hand, some industries were handicapped by lack of materials arising out of the demands of the defence program. At the same time other industries, particularly those producing consumer goods, were operating well below capacity. The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease cut off exports of our livestock and meat to the United States.
During the course of 1952 the Canadian economy adjusted itself to the defence effort and achieved balance at a high level of activity. The establishment of new capacity in raw material producing industries helped to eliminate shortages of key materials such as steel and cement. Internationally, the supply situation improved to the point where it became possible to get along without international allocation of most essential materials. Just a few scarce materials remain under international allocation.
Here in Canada consumer buying gradually increased during the year and gave a substantial boost to employment in the industries producing both hard and soft goods. In the

Supply-Trade and Commerce final quarter of 1952, for example, about 14 per cent more goods passed over retail counters than in the same quarter of 1951.
To show the extent of the improvement let me particularize for a moment. Comparing the latter part of 1952 with the same period of 1951, production levels were running about 20 per cent higher in the case of motor vehicles; 67 per cent higher in the case of refrigerators; 92 per cent in the case of washing machines; and 135 per cent in the case of electric stoves. And now we have a new television industry which sold about
75,000	units from the factories in the fourth quarter of 1952.
The suspension of consumer credit regulations and the removal of special excise taxes in the budget of 1952 helped to stimulate consumer buying. Those restrictions had been essential at an earlier period, and they were taken off as soon as they were no longer needed. But the more important reason for the upturn in consumption was the steady increase in personal incomes and the levelling off and decline in consumer prices. The statisticians tell me that during 1952 the per capita average real income of wage and salary earners increased by about 9 per cent, a 7 per cent increase in money incomes and a 2 per cent drop in consumer prices. There was also some reduction in the rate of personal saving, that is a higher proportion of incomes was spent rather than saved in 1952 compared with 1951, which added still further to consumer buying.
By the end of 1952 most of the soft spots previously in evidence had disappeared, although a few others developed during the year. A reduced demand for wood pulp brought about a reduced pulpwood cut this season. The winter shutdown affected a large amount of construction work under way in outlying areas. On the whole, however, market forces are in good balance and, with few exceptions Canadian industries are working at close to capacity.
As a result total output, the gross national production, reached $23 billion, compared with $21-4 billion in 1951. The physical change, after eliminating the effect of prices, was about a 6 per cent increase. Even after excluding the effects of the phenomenal crops harvested on the prairies, the increase compared favourably with that achieved in any previous post-war years. It was a year of notable progress in standards of living for the Canadian people. But it was also a year devoted to the development of our resources and to the building up of capacity to make possible an even higher standard of living in the future. Capital investment absorbed no less than 22 per cent of our national output.

So great indeed has been the rate of capital investment in post-war years that many people have wondered how long it could continue. Yet each year when we survey the intentions of businessmen and public bodies we find that they are planning to spend more on capital account than they did the year before. This year is no exception. There is every reason to believe that investment outlays will show a further significant increase in 1953.
During the past two years an increased proportion of capital outlays has been directed toward expansion in industries of particular importance to Canada's over-all preparedness such as mineral and hydro developments, strategic raw material processing and new plants for the production of defence and other heavy equipment. While this expansion of basic industry is still proceeding, some of the major programs undertaken within the last two or three years are well on their way to completion. For example, expenditures for new capacity in the steel and chemical industries is expected to be lower in 1953 than in the preceding year.
The substantial development taking place is certain to involve extensive supplementary investment in services and other related fields. In view of the limited resources available in 1951 and 1952 much of this secondary expansion has been delayed. This postponement was encouraged by government measures specifically designed to make way for more urgent projects. Meanwhile, productive capacity in building materials industries has been increasing and in addition supplies from abroad have become more readily available. The deferred depreciation measure, restrictions on the use of steel for construction, and other measures designed to discourage less essential investment have therefore been removed. There are now indications that outlays for housing, trade establishments and so forth will be considerably increased in 1953.
In total it is now estimated that the 1953 capital expenditure program will involve outlays of $5-4 billion compared with $5 [DOT] 1 billion expended last year. This estimate is based for the most part on a recent survey of the investment intentions of business, institutions and governments. Some weeks ago I tabled two reports which give details of these forecasts.
If investment plans for 1953 are realized, this will be the sixth consecutive year in which capital outlays have reached more than 20 per cent of total national production. Some upturn in capital expenditure following the establishment of the new rearmament

objectives was to have been expected. However, as I have previously indicated, we have now made a good deal of progress in adjusting to these new goals. For capital outlays still to be increasing substantiates the view that Canada's present expansion is not based on temporary boom conditions. It is not a flash in the pan. Instead, it reflects the growing diversity and adaptability of Canada's industry and the capacity to produce economically an increasing proportion of the world's requirements.
It is important to note that whereas much of the investment spending made in the immediate post-war years was for replacement needs, a much larger proportion of today's investment represents new additions to capacity, based on the expectation of adequate markets for many years to come. Future markets can never, of course, be fully assured. Canadian industries remain vulnerable to dislocating influences, particularly from abroad, and future growth will depend to a very large extent upon continued progress toward sound and vigorous world trade.
Now let me turn to the record of Canada's external trade. Exports continued to advance last year. They amounted in total in 1952 to $4-4 billion, an increase of $400 million over 1951, the previous highest year. The total value of imports in 1952 remained at about the same level as the year before.
Each time in recent years that I have reported further advances in our exports, I have been asked whether we are really selling larger quantities of goods or whether the increased values may not simply reflect higher prices. In 1952 the volume of exports increased by even more than their total value. Export prices actually declined during the year, although not by any more than 1 or 2 per cent on the average. Since 1950 the total value of our exports has risen by about 39 per cent and the physical volume by 23 per cent, a remarkable and sustained record. Of course not all exports have fared equally well during this period. There have been some real difficulties in the export of manufactured goods, although this has been more than made up by strong demand in the domestic market.
As I have said, livestock producers experienced a major setback in 1952 owing to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. The ban on exports to the United States has now been lifted and normal trade is being resumed. In the meantime, many adverse effects of the meat surplus situation have been avoided by the use of price supports and by special arrangements made to deal with surplus stocks.
17, 1953
Supply-Trade and Commerce
On the other hand, grain producers have benefited from a record crop accompanied by a strong world market for their product. In the present crop year we expect to export all the wheat that can be handled by our transportation and storage facilities. The continuing world-wide demand for our major export products and the relative stability of our export prices provide evidence of the basic strength of Canada's position in world trade. This strength has been created in large part by sound policies, and it has buoyed us up during a period when many other countries have suffered setbacks. By wise though sometimes unpopular measures we have succeeded in avoiding most of the damage that inflation has inflicted upon the trade of many other countries, which is one reason our dollar is so strong.
During 1952 major downward adjustments occurred in the prices of many of the basic commodities and foodstuffs which move in world trade. Price declines of as much as one-third or one-half were quite common in 1952. As examples of commodities thus affected I might mention rubber, tin, cotton and wool. Canadian importers and consumers have benefited from these reduced prices. On the average, the prices of imports fell by 12 per cent during 1952. Our exports, with a few notable exceptions such as lead, zinc and lumber, have been relatively exempt from drastic price adjustments, which is evidence in itself of the demand which exists for our goods.
Two or three years ago there began to be a good deal of concern expressed that too large a proportion of our exports were being marketed in the United States. The totals were satisfactory but perhaps we were getting too many of our export eggs in one basket. As Minister of Trade and Commerce I stated on a number of occasions that this situation was mainly a reflection of the financial difficulties through which the sterling area countries and western European countries were passing. There has at no time been any lack of desire in overseas countries to obtain Canadian goods.
In my view we have been fortunate in Canada, during this period, to have the great markets of the United States open and receptive to our goods. We have certainly taken advantage of our opportunities in that direction, and Canadian exports to the United States have risen to a level of $2-3 billion.
During these years the government has done everything possible to encourage and assist the recovery of our exports to those countries overseas which are our traditional customers. I am pleased to say that almost all of the $400 million increase which took place

Supply-Trade and Commerce in our exports in 1952 went to countries overseas. Very little of the increase took place in exports to the United States, where we just about maintained our position last year and even improved it a little bit. Consequently the percentage of our exports going to the United States has declined steadily, which I am sure all hon. members will agree is a healthy sign. In 1950, 65 per cent of our total exports went to the United States; in
1951	the figure was down to 59 per cent and in 1952 it was down to 54 per cent. Our efforts to diversify our exports have been paying off.
It has been encouraging to see the way in which the trade and financial position of th6 United Kingdom has improved in recent months. Such improvement is a good thing for Canada from every point of view. Canada participated fully in the recent commonwealth economic conference, as hon. members are aware. We may be greatly encouraged also by the increasing amount of international agreement about what needs to be done to solve the trade and financial problems of the sterling area and western Europe. Many of the countries concerned are showing signs of moving in the right direction.
In our attempts to overcome barriers to trade we have not by any means as yet had all the success we would wish for, particularly in regard to the British countries. Many of our manufactured goods are still excluded from overseas markets because of import restrictions. Nevertheless, in 1952 the value, quantity and proportion of our exports to British countries did increase and for the first time their value amounted to over $1 billion. Greater shipments of wheat and metals to the United Kingdom account for most of this increase.
Canadian imports from the United Kingdom were relatively low in the first few months of
1952	but have been increasing lately with the upsurge in consumer buying in this country. I am glad to see that the United Kingdom have been able to increase their sales to us of many types of machinery and that their sales to the United States are increasing. It has been said before, but it bears repeating, that there is a large and continuing market in this country for many goods which the United Kingdom can supply in greater quantities.
We have substantially improved our sales to Europe, Latin America and other foreign countries overseas. The total of these exports increased by $240 million to just short of $1 billion. Germany has increased its Canadian purchases substantially so that it is now the second largest European market for our

products. Here again wheat accounted for much of the increase. Most other European countries are now buying more Canadian goods, including Belgium, our largest European market.
In Asia the most notable increases took place in our exports to Japan. Sales to Japan rose to the point where they were in excess of $100 million in 1952. From the Canadian point of view the increasing importance of the Japanese market has become more and more apparent in each recent year.
In Latin America also we have expanded our sales. Whereas in Europe we are largely selling raw materials, in Latin America manufactured goods constitute a much greater proportion of the total. Exports of such essential manufactures as trucks, machinery and electrical equipment to Latin America have all increased. As I have already reported to the house, there is no doubt that there are great possibilities for further sales in Latin America of manufactured goods of all kinds. To make the most of these opportunities it is necessary for Canadian businessmen to make personal contacts. There is lots of competition, but the opportunities are very real.
Canada and the United States continue to be each other's best customers. This extensive trade is both a cause and a result of the cordial commercial relations which have been developed over the years. Both countries have fostered the development of trade, across our joint borders and with the world at large. Both Canada and the United States have attempted as much as possible to solve numerous trade problems, not by restrictive measures but by reducing trade barriers and expanding the opportunities to trade. With the recent change of administration in the United States government, I feel confident and hopeful that problems of commercial relations between Canada and the United States can continue to be dealt with along these lines.
This is not to say that there have been no problems or differences between Canada and the United States. At every appropriate opportunity the government has made clear to the government of the United States that basic principles are being infringed by the imposition of import controls upon dairy products in the United States. We have made clear, furthermore, the importance we attach to the passage of customs simplification legislation in the United States, to facilitate trade and to fulfil the agreements which were entered into at Geneva in 1947.
Negotiations of profound importance for the future of trade and commercial policy will have to be conducted during 1953. Consideration will have to be given by the major

trading countries to the future of the international program which has been established under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Canada and the United States have helped themselves and the world as a whole through the negotiation of extensive trade agreements, before the war in 1935 and 1938, and since the war under GATT at Geneva in 1947 and at Torquay in 1951.. The unprecedented flow of trade between Canada and the United States today is conducted in accordance with the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
Since the tariff undertakings of the general agreement on tariffs and trade are firmly bound only until the end of 1953, decisions will have to be made amongst the countries concerned as to what further steps to take to safeguard the future of international trade. There may be a further opportunity to take steps forward in the reduction of tariffs and the elimination of trade restrictions, as an alternative to moving in the other direction. The interest of Canada in this matter is perfectly clear, because we require other markets to be open to our goods on an expanding scale.
The role of the United States will be a crucial one and, as always in such circumstances, I am sure that constructive American leadership will not be lacking when it is needed.
Over the years Canada has become one of the world's most important trading nations, and our standing in that respect has never been higher than it is today. That this is so is due primarily to the capacity and enterprise of the Canadian people and to the extent and variety of the resources which they have at their command. Government policies, too, have played an important role, and I wish to refer briefly to some of the trade promotional activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce, particularly to the work of the trade commissioner service which is well known to many of you in a general way.
This is both an old and a new service. Its origins go back to the very early days of the department, but it was not until the period immediately following world war I that it was built up and organized on such a scale as to give Canada a really competent trade service in most of the world's principal commercial centres. During the ten or twelve years following world war I the extension of this service was carried out in a vigorous way. In fact Canada, by reason of circumstances which were peculiar to our national development, reversed the usual order of events. We were more or less compelled to equip ourselves with strong and world-wide
17, 1953
Supply*-Trade and Commerce trade representation before we had made more than a modest start on the establishment of our political or diplomatic foreign service. It was Canada's rapid commercial growth that accounted for this marked departure from the ordinary sequence of events.
Our first venture into foreign representation on a large scale having been dictated chiefly by our urgent commercial needs, it was natural that special attention should be given, and was given, to developing a service that would be as efficient as we could make it from the trade promotion standpoint. The recruits to this service were selected and trained entirely with that object in view.
The young men who came into the trade commissioner service did so with a commercial career in mind. Emphasis was1 laid upon their having some business experience to start with, on top of which they were put through a thorough course of training before being posted abroad. Great importance was attached to having them gain a firsthand knowledge of Canada's major export industries by actual visits to plants in all parts of the country and by becoming personally acquainted with the export managers and other business executives through whom their subsequent work abroad could be made most effective. That close contact between the trade commissioners and businessmen throughout Canada has been responsible, more than any other factor, for building up the reputation of our trade commissioner service and the good will which it has enjoyed in business circles for many years past.
That reputation is not just local, for I believe it is widely recognized that Canada's commercial representation abroad is not excelled by that of any other country. We intend to keep it that way, and it is a matter for congratulation that whatever administration has been in office in Canada at any time during the past 30 or 40 years, there has never been any difference of policy, or of practice either, in regard to the importance of seeing to it that we support and maintain this service on a most efficient basis.
It is, as I have said, both an old and a new service-new in the sense that at the close of world war II we had a pressing problem to deal with in reopening offices abroad that had been closed and in finding personnel to man these as well as a number of new offices which have had to be established during the past seven or eight years. In fact we have virtually had to re-create the trade commissioner service, but we have now reached the stage where we can truthfully

Supply-Trade and Commerce say that it is not only back on its feet but in better shape than ever.
Three new offices were opened during 1952 at New Orleans, Ciudad Trujillo and Beirut. These offices will serve territories which we have reason to believe will afford good opportunities for the expansion of Canada's exports. We now have 51 offices in 40 countries, manned by 102 trade commissioners and assistant trade commissioners. I take particular satisfaction in pointing out that during the course of rebuilding this service we have paid great attention to the need for men whose training has been specialized along the lines of promoting the exports of agricultural and fisheries products.
Coupled with this greater degree of specialization, we now have the advantage of a foreign commercial service in which there is a much improved balance as between the older and more experienced personnel and the younger group who, in another few years, will be stepping up into the senior positions.
Apart from the trade commissioner service there are, of course, other divisions of the department, centred here at Ottawa, that are responsible for carrying on important trade promotional activities, notably the international trade relations division, which is concerned especially with trade agreements and trade negotiations with other countries, and the commodities division, whose officers provide an essential link between the business community at home and the trade commissioners abroad.
May I close with a word regarding the Canadian international trade fair. This fair has been held annually since its inception in 1948. The 1952 fair was, we believe, the most successful that has been held to date, although in point of size it still fell somewhat short of the opening fair in 1948. We are now well advanced in the preparations for the 1953 fair, to be held this coming June, and I am glad to be able to state that this will be, without exception, much the largest fair that we have had yet. Moreover it will have, on the exhibit side, a good division between the amounts of exhibit space taken respectively by Canadian firms and by firms from other countries. Exhibit space for the 1953 fair is now at a premium. We have reached the stage at which, from the standpoint of improving the fair as a business undertaking, we are having to give at least as much attention to building up the attendance of bona fide business visitors as to the attracting of either Canadian or foreign exhibitors. This Canadian trade fair has already won wide recognition abroad, and I think we can safely say that its success represents one of the outstanding advances made by Canada

in many years in the field of international trade promotion.

Montreal, P.Q.
Dear Major Prefontaine:
Following on the meeting of your group with the Hon. Mr. Lapointe, representing the Prime Minister, your representations regarding compensation to prisoners of war on account of maltreatment were examined by the government, and I now have to inform you of their conclusions.
While your proposals were considered as sympathetically as possible, it is not felt that you have adduced any arguments which require the government to modify its previously announced decision, that is, to put into effect the recommendations made by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, the commissioner on war claims.
The proposition which your group advanced is that, as the prisoners of war who were interned in Japanese camps in the Far East have been paid compensation at a per diem rate, similar payments should also be made to those who were prisoners of war in German and Italian camps, as it is your contention that all of the latter group suffered maltreatment.
It is the view of the commissioner, in which the government concurs, that there was a substantial difference in the treatment of prisoners of war by the Japanese on the one hand and by the Germans and Italians on the other hand. However, the relatively few prisoners who were held in custody by the gestapo and other organizations declared illegal at Nuremberg are to be treated the same as those in Japanese operated camps.
The commissioner's reasons for arriving at this conclusion in regard to Japanese controlled camps are set forth in detail on pages 41 and 49 of his report, and seem to the government to be valid. On page 50 of the report he gives evidence from the "British Hand Book" to the effect that conditions in the German and Italian camps were not such as to support any presumption of general maltreatment.
The British government, by paying a small lump sum grant to those who were interned by the Japanese, and by not doing so to those who were interned by the Germans and Italians, has acted in conformity with the finding that conditions in the two theatres were vastly different. This finding is confirmed by the following facts which are on record as a result of the post-war experience of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Canadian pension commission with prisoners of war from both theatres.
As for the Far Eastern prisoners of war, their food was so limited that nearly all who survived showed clinical evidence of avitaminosis while in camp. A high percentage had also clinical evidence of dysentery, etc. Roughly 20 per cent of all Far Eastern prisoners of war suffered permanent damage as the result of avitaminosis. Autopsies on a number of deceased Far Eastern prisoners of war who had certain symptoms but no physical signs of disability proved that they suffered from avitaminosis. Records of the rehabilitation and welfare services branches of the D.V.A. show that a high percentage of survivors have had occupational difficulties and impaired general health.
On the other hand, as regards European prisoners of war, there is no record of any avitaminosis occurring while in camp, or discovered subsequent to liberation. While there is evidence of intestinal infestation (dysentery, etc.) it is much lower than among the Far Eastern prisoners of war. In the summer of 1946 instructions were issued that all prisoners of war were to have a complete physical examination including an X-ray of their chest and any other indicated special examinations. There have been no indications as a result of these examinations or subsequent surveys that any considerable number of prisoners of war in the European theatre suffered impairment.
Canadian army statistics of death from nonbattle causes, while prisoners of war in the two theatres, are, however, probably more decisive than any other evidence. In the campaigns in Italy, Sicily, and North West Europe and in the Dieppe operations some 4,005 unwounded prisoners of war were taken, and of these only 37 died from non-battle casualties while prisoners of war-a death rate of less than one in a hundred.

In Hong Kong, however, 1,289 unwounded prisoners of war were taken; of these 264 died of non-battle causes or a death rate of approximately one in five. These figures speak for themselves, indicating the difference in conditions in prisoner of war camps in the Far East and in Europe.
Your group advanced arguments that all prisoners of war in German and Italian camps suffered more or less from poor shelter, interruption of mail, the fear of death and various indignities. It is not felt that any concrete evidence has been offered to offset the conclusions of the commissioner, and that in any case hardships of that kind cannot be said to entitle those who have suffered them to receive a payment which would be denied to the front-line soldier who is in greater danger of death and at the same time frequently suffers equal or greater hardships.
It was represented that individual prisoners of war would have considerable difficulty in proving maltreatment through lack of evidence, and lack of facility in expression. In order to eliminate any unfairness on this score, the government decided to make the

services of the pensions advocates of the Department of Veterans Affairs available to any prisoner of war who may wish to make a claim in respect of maltreatment. These officials will be well able to obtain the available evidence and advocate the claims effectively. A considerable number of former prisoners of war have already taken advantage of these facilities, and it is hoped that all who feel that they have a claim for compensation for maltreatment will do so.
In conclusion I am instructed to say, that after most careful and sympathetic consideration, the government feels that the proposals for settling the claims to compensation of prisoners of war laid down by the commissioner and set forth in the report dated 25th February 1952, are essentially sound and equitable, and that any prisoner of war, having a valid claim for maltreatment, will be able to obtain the compensation to which he is entitled.
Yours sincerely,
